speechtext:
that Bill C-237, an act to amend the Interest Act (calculation of credit card interest), be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee E.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to amend the Interest Act. The calculation of interest and how it is to be calculated is a matter of federal jurisdiction which we have not dealt with sufficiently. The bill deals with the calculation and the terms of calculation of interest rates on credit cards. It does not limit the interest rate or control interest rates, it merely determines how interest is to be calculated and it does that for the following reasons.
First, it is a bill designed to make the calculation of interest possible and provable. Second, it is a bill to standardize the calculation of interest so that consumers can compare the interest rates they are charged on credit cards. Third, it is a bill designed to prevent unconscionable double dipping by some credit card companies charging interest on money for which they have already received a payment or a fee for lending in the first place.
We are all in love today with our plastic. There is not a Canadian who does not go around with plastic in all cases. We have on average something like two and a half credit cards per individual. We all love our plastic.
Before plastic it was necessary for us to pay our bills in cash. If you did not have the cash you could not pay or
you paid your bills with a cheque. If the merchant would not take your cheque then you could not buy. If you had a good arrangement with your merchant he might give you credit but you would pay the merchant off at the end of the month or whenever.
The incidence of plastic now makes it possible for people to buy goods and services anywhere in the world where your plastic is good.
As an aside I suppose we would all be better off in some senses if we did not have plastic because we would not run up some of the debts we run up but our world moves because we are able to move money quickly from one person to another. The plastic makes that possible.
Those who issue credit cards get their emolument or get paid for their service in three fashions. First they charge what is called a merchant fee. A merchant fee is really a method whereby the merchant factors his account receivable, because he has not been paid in cash, to a bank or a credit card company. The bank or credit card company pays him for the receivable. The bank or credit card company then bills its customer who is the holder of the card for the good or service at the time of payment. The bank takes a discount on the amount of the cost of the good as a merchant fee.
If you buy something for $100 and the merchant fee is $3 the merchant gets $97. The bank or credit card company collects when it collects its fee of $100 at the appropriate time and therefore makes $3 for supplying the credit or looking after the credit.
The second method of payment or emolument to the credit card company is a user fee. Those fees vary all over the place. Some credit card companies charge an annual fee. American Express for example charges $75 on their green card. Some companies charge a monthly fee. Some charge $1 a month, $12 a year or 50 cents a transaction. These are user fees and they vary all over the place. It depends on the merchandising of the card and how the company wants to handle it.

Private Members' Business
All companies charge interest in one form or another and calculate it in a different way on the amount outstanding on their cards. Some companies like the Bank of Montreal on its MasterCard do not charge any user fees. It charges merchant fees and interest on the card.
The American Express or Amex green card charges a very substantial up front user fee and a merchant fee but only charges interest when the account is in default and then it collects interest on the money and usually at the same time terminates the credit because it takes the position on the green card part of its business that it is not in the business of lending money. It is in the business of facilitating purchases. Interest is on default only. On default the card becomes a cancelled card. They sue to collect their money and at that point demand interest.
I wish to explain this bill and how it will work. At the present time interest is charged by people in a different and peculiar fashion. To understand interest and how it is charged one must understand merchant fees and why they occur.
Merchant fees can be anywhere between 1.5 per cent and 5 per cent of the sale price, depending on the contract the merchant has with the person who allows him to use the card. It can be the bank or whoever.
Say for example I deal with a merchant who is a jeweller and I decide to buy a $100 bauble for my wife. Suppose the merchant has a fee of 3 per cent. I sign my Visa card and agree to pay $100 for the bauble. I take the bauble and the merchant takes my Visa slip and he immediately deposits it in his bank account. The bank credits him not with $100 but $97. He has $97 immediately in his bank account. He does not have to worry about my credit. He does not have to worry about a cheque that might bounce. He is able to make a sale because I did not have $100 in my pocket. I could not have bought the bauble so he has made a sale that otherwise he would not have made.
The merchant is happy because he has $97 in cash and I suppose he has calculated the cost of supplying that credit in the purchase price of the bauble.
When the bank collects it obviously collects the $100. The merchant fee profit on the transaction to the bank is $3.1 suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that merchant fee
represents interest on the advance of money to the merchant. That is what it is. It is a pre-calculated interest charge for the use of credit and the merchant has paid for that credit because the credit has been to his benefit.
Suppose I made that purchase from the jeweller on November 15. At that time the merchant got his $97 and the bank paid out $97. If it was a Visa account that I have they may bill everything up to the end of November. On December 2 they will send out a bill to me dated December 2 which says that if I pay by December 211 can just pay $100 and that will be the end of it.
In most cases that is the end of it. At least half of the people who buy on credit cards pay their cards off within the credit period. In this particular example the credit period runs to December 21.1 have that period of time to pay the bill. If I pay it on time that is all there is to it.
Suppose I do not have $100. I only have $50 and I pay $50 on the account which leaves $50 still outstanding. One would think in decency that the bank has received $3 interest on the money to December 21 and and if they get $50 in that period then they would only charge interest on that $50 from December 21 to the next payment date. That is what you would think would be decent. That would be the ordinary calculation of interest on what ordinarily ought to happen.
But oh, no, they play a different game.
This is the fault that must be corrected. This is what this bill is about. Instead of treating $50 as something they have, they proceed to say that they have not been paid in full, and therefore are entitled to charge interest on $100.
Even though they have interest on $100, they charge interest on $100 at their rate, we will say at 18 per cent per annum, not from December 21, not from December 2, but from November 15. Interest on $100 from November 15 until December 21 works out to about $1.80. Right off the bat, they add $1.80 to the account and then they get $50 and are still owed $50.
They say it is plus $1.80 for interest, but they want even more than that because when they send their bill out on January 2, they calculate interest on $50 from December 21 until January 21 and that comes to another 75 cents or 76 cents or so. On January 2, they send a bill for $52.86, giving them another calculation of interest.
December 2, 1991

The bill is designed to stop that fault. The bill says: "Interest on a credit card account shall be calculated monthly as it accrues and where unpaid when due, such interest shall be compounded monthly from the date that payment was due". In this case, payment is due on December 21 and interest should be calculated from the date payment is due.
When they send out their bill on January 2, they should send out a bill for interest from December 21 to January 21 representing a cost of approximately 76 cents or a bill for $50.76. That is really the compensation they are entitled to on the amount of that advance.
What has been happening, and happening with increasing frequency, is that card companies have been doubly dipping the consumer. First of all, they dip the consumer, indirectly I admit, when they get a merchant fee to cover the cost of carrying the credit to the end of the credit period.
Then they come back if they are not paid in full and want interest all over again on the same money. This bill is designed to prevent that happening. It is designed to make it possible for people to calculate the interest outstanding.
Right now, while my example only had me buying one article in the month, I might have bought a series of articles on November 2, 14, 15, 27 and so on. In each case, the bank would have calculated back to the date of purchase. I could not conceivably determine the amount of that bank calculation.
When the bill arrives with interest, I just have to assume that it is correct under the current system. Under the system proposed in this bill, I will know when I pay $50 on account, what is the balance owing on my account. I will be able, with straight long form arithmetic if necessary, to calculate the interest that should be due when my bill comes again to be paid in January, to be paid by January 21.
For the first time consumers, if this bill should pass, will have the opportunity to determine what interest they are paying for the advance made on their plastic by the issuer of the plastic card.
I commend this bill to the House. I think this matter has to be dealt with. Institutions have tried to avoid
Private Members' Business
dealing with it. I suspect today that the government in its usual fashion will put up one speaker after another to say that it somehow interferes with business.
Well, it is about time we allowed business to operate sensibly and fairly. It is about time that the calculation of interest was controlled in the same manner for everyone and this bill attempts to do that.

Mr. Speaker, it is good to see you so chipper so early in the morning at the beginning of a week. You are setting the tone for the entire week and it is good to see that.
I rise today to support Bill C-237 put forward by my hon. colleague. He has put a lot of work into this bill. Over the last few months I have had to read-and I have to say it has not been painful-a lot of his past press releases as well as testimony in committee when he was chair of the finance committee. The committee brought in a report, I believe it was in 1988, dealing with credit cards generally. In 1989 the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs revisited this entire issue. Since the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs Committee is now dealing with the issue again, this bill is a topical issue.
At the outset I want to indicate to the hon. member that the issues he raises are serious and affect almost every single consumer in Canada. A lot of times private members' bills put forward in this place have a very limited application and there are not a lot of people out there who are affected. I dare say there is probably not a member of Parliament and there are very few adults in Canada that do not have credit cards. The startling statistics are that there are about 27 million bank cards out there and only about 18 million adults in Canada. In addition to that, there is probably another 30 or 40 million department store cards.
If you really want to look at a bill that has broad implications for every consumer in Canada, this certainly is one of them. The member also brings with him a tremendous degree of credibility when he deals with financial issues. He is not one of these Johnny-come-latelys to the vast and dark tunnel of financial institutions. He has been dealing with them in this and previous Parliaments for a long time. I want to commend him for his perseverance at this point in his career, in continuing to dog this particular issue because he knows that fundamental change is needed.

December 2, 1991
Private Members' Business
I want to underline this point. The hon. member indicated that the current way credit card issuers calculate interest is pretty bizarre. It is fine to say that consumers should understand what is the effective rate of interest being charged. I will bet you that if you pulled aside any dozen individuals in this Chamber and asked them how the credit card companies calculate interest, unless they have been involved either in the finance committee deliberations of 1988 or involved in the consumer and corporate affairs committee deliberations in 1989, they would not know. They would not have any idea. It is almost like life insurance policies. How many people out there actually know what all the small print means on their life insurance policies? I do not think even most life insurance salesmen know.
It is the same thing when you come to credit card interest rates. My hon. colleague is quite correct. What happens is clear. The credit card issuer states that there will be a a grace period and if the balance is paid off during that grace period there will be no interest charged. That is basically it. We heard from the Royal Bank and the Bank of Montreal just two weeks ago that one-half of all the banks cards, Visa, MasterCards in circulation have an average unpaid balance of an of $1,000 every month. So we are not dealing with a little bit of money, we are dealing with about 15 million cards with an average balance of $1,000 every month.
I want to read a letter that I just received in my office on November 27 addressed to the Hon. Pierre Blais. I am not going to indicate the author of this letter because it deals with some financial information that he may not wish to have disclosed.
I want to read this letter because it certainly puts bank interest charges in perspective. It says that his October 1991 Visa account had an outstanding charge of $2,101.72. It was his intention to pay off his account in full, as he always did. He was a good consumer who paid his balance off every month. Isn't he lucky that he has the money to do that. However, through an error, he issued a cheque for $2,001.72 and he enclosed a copy of the cheque. That left a carryover amount of $100.
He thought he had paid the $2,101.72 off, but he left a balance of $100 in the way he wrote the cheque. He is one of those guys who are lucky enough to have the money to pay off that bloody card at the end of every month.
On his November 1991 account, of which I have a copy, he now finds an interest charge of $50.57 on a carryover amount of $100. He has paid over 50 per cent interest on his balance. You do not get interest relief at all unless you pay every cent off, every penny of the money that you have charged. If you do not pay it all off within the grace period you are going to get nailed for the interest on money that you have already paid off. The full amount. Nothing could more clearly illustrate the point that my hon. colleague has made.
In 1988 my hon. colleague put forward Bill C-238. The bill sought to do the same thing this one is doing. It is trying to put some sanity into the marketplace when dealing with financial institutions, and regarding large credit card issuers, it is trying to standardize the method of interest calculation so that consumers will be able to know. It is pretty difficult. It is like going into a dark corner where there are 12 hissing snakes and trying to pick out the one that is not poisonous. It is the same thing right now with consumers who are trying to deal with the different rates of interest calculated by various card issuers.
My colleague has put forward a bill to which the government could easily assent. The financial institutions may not like it, but they usually do not like it when they have regulations that in effect make them more accountable, not just to Parliament but to the consumers out there.
As one of my colleagues said a little earlier, credit cards derive their money from three different areas: the transaction fee they charge the retailer, the interest rates and user fees.
If anybody out there is about to start crying in their cups for the major credit card issuers in this country, I just want to let them all know that the consumer and corporate affairs committee, in some of its deliberations a few weeks ago, was questioning two of the major banks in Canada. We wanted to find out why the banks had to keep primary interest rates a full 12 percentage points above the treasury bill rate. What the banks had indicated is that it was because of their loan losses. The country is in a recession, 40,000 consumers have gone bankrupt across the country in the last 10 months, a horrendous figures, and it was because of loan losses on Visa and MasterCard accounts.
December 2, 1991

I was very particular and I said: "Does that mean you are losing money?" They said: "No, it is just that our losses are high". I said: "So what you are telling me is that on one of the three components where you make your money, you have to charge 12 per cent more because you have not made enough money?" Is that what you are trying to tell us?' They did not nod yes, but by their silence and by their stoic look, the answer had to be yes, it could not be anything else but yes.
When the banks come out, as they would if this bill were adopted, and say this is unfair and unduly restricts the marketplace and there should be an allowance through which we can deal with these complex financial calculations outside of the realm of Parliament and regulation, I just want to indicate that we have just gone through one of the worst recessions on record, a very difficult recession. The Royal Bank is a very good bank and I do not get any letters from Royal Bank managers. It is a very good financial institution. It serves its shareholders well. It makes a lot of money for them and banks are in the business of making money. The Royal Bank last year made about $923 million in net income. The Royal Bank this year is probably going to make either a little below that or, if the next month is better, it may even hit a billion dollars. That is a lot of money.
The Bank of Montreal, a very aggressive bank, has gone out there, dropped rates and it is a very competitive institution. I credit the management of that institution for shaking up all of our financial institutions in Canada by its aggressive behaviour. The Bank of Montreal, in the middle of a recession, has posted record profits. When we start dealing with-
What have they all paid in taxes?
My hon. colleague from Broadview-Greenwood asks what they have paid in taxes.
On whose backs?

On whose backs have they done it.
If we look at this bill in perspective, it seeks to give the consumer some relief. It puts into the marketplace a
Private Members' Business
regime which is standardized so that the consumer knows once and for all exactly how his interest is going to be calculated.
It also says to the large financial institutions that issue these cards that we are going to keep an eye on them. We do not want to make them unprofitable, but we do not want to leave them out there so highly unregulated that the consumer is going to suffer.
We in the Liberal Party believe this is the type of measure that will look after both interests and you can look after both interests.
Canada needs strong financial institutions. As well, we need strong consumer protection from undue gouging and from some practices some might consider to be a bit of collusion.
In conclusion, I want to commend my hon. colleague. He has tremendous tenacity. He is like a dog with a bone and he is not going to let this one go. I want to let him know that some on this side of the House treat his perseverance with a great deal of respect. We on this side of the House think that this bill goes a very significant way in ensuring that in the complex area of financial institutions, the setting of credit card interest rates through all three of the areas we talked about before are open to more public scrutiny and are more accountable to those 22 million credit card holders across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I guess the hon. member for Don Valley is going to hit a home run today. This close to Christmas perhaps he merits it because I too would like to speak on his bill in support of it.
As a consumer advocate for close to 23 years I too have seen consumers gouged by excessive credit card rates and unfair credit card practices. When we look at the establishment of interest rates, it is no wonder that we, the members of the consumer affairs committee, along with my colleague from Cape Breton, would like to see a serious approach taken to bringing down these interest rates. Whether it is a floating cap or other measures, there have to be some serious measures taken right now in order to prevent consumers in this country from getting gouged.

Private Members' Business
When we are talking about gouging through credit card interest rates as well as practices, you have to look at the two differently. With respect to interest rates, my party and other parties I think have been in favour of having a floating cap. This is not spoken to in the hon. member's bill. It is unfortunate because the consumers affairs committee twice, in 1989 and prior, recommended that there be a floating cap. That was an all party committee, Conservatives, Liberals and NDP. It was just common sense, gros bon sens.
I am sure the hon. member probably agrees with the government. It did not wish to see a floating cap on interest rates. That is unfortunate because it is a very serious problem, I think even more serious than this double dipping problem relating to the approach it takes to calculating the interest rate.
If we take a look at the interest rate structure right now, the card companies are going to say: "We need every opportunity in order to cut down on these fraudulent claims or on these people who are delinquent in paying".
I am going to stop for a minute because of the noise from the other side. It is very difficult for me to even hear what I am saying.

speechtext: Order, please. If you wish to carry on a conversation, would you carry it on behind the curtain. It is very difficult to hear the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, it is especially because credit card issuers explain high interest rates by the large number of unpaid accounts and the many false claims. But this is not the consumers' problem-it is the credit card issuers'. They choose their card holders in a rather strange way. People who were $250,000 in debt and went bankrupt were solicited to become card holders the next day. They are approached by credit card issuers like the banks and, in one specific case, American Express, as reported by journalist Pierre Berton. So these people are always being solicited, whether they were bankrupt or not. Of course, this may be a way to get more customers, but it forces people like you and me and many other Canadians who pay every month to pay more on account of those who do not pay. I find that is neither right nor fair.
The interest rates are unacceptable. As my hon. colleague said, they vary from 19 to 20 per cent in some cases, with the banks, to 25 per cent for department stores and other companies and even 30 per cent for American Express. Yes, 30 per cent. We should find out whether the companies are really doing so badly that a bill like the one presented by the hon. member could bankrupt them. Would they suffer large losses as a result? I do not believe so. I simply believe that it would be fair to require these companies to act responsibly towards their customers by setting acceptable interest rates. A difference of 12 points between the bank rate and the current interest rate is really enormous. If it were cut in half, to 4, 4.5 or 5 per cent, it would at least mean that the customer could obtain justice. I call that simple justice.
It is true that the credit card issuers today make huge profits except, perhaps, interestingly enough, American Express with the Optima card, which was a big fiasco. In the United States, some people like hotel and restaurant owners are really unhappy with the Optima Card. American Express probably needs a 30 per cent interest rate today because it lost so much in the past. But I find rates of 25 per cent and 20 per cent for the banks, department stores and other companies really unacceptable, especially in view of the profits of financial institutions, particularly banks, recently.
So as for interest rates, I find that my hon. colleague should show some courage, independence and even tenacity and really demand that interest rates be capped at a certain level and that banks and other companies be required to respect that ceiling.
When I spoke with the bank representatives who appeared before the Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations, the representatives of the Royal Bank and the Bank of Montreal said, or rather admitted, because they did not want to say so at first, that in the past, in the 1960s, interest rates were capped, although perhaps the hon. member for Don Valley may not have been aware of that. And I asked the bank representatives whether they had any particular difficulty with the interest rate ceiling. They told me that they did not, as you can check. It was not a problem then. Maybe today, 30 years later, there might be a problem, I don't know. But in the past, when interest rates were capped, they did not have that problem.
December 2, 1991

So I would be inclined to think that the banks and other institutions would not have very great problems if interest rates were capped.
A second point that I would like to raise, besides the need for a limit on interest rates, is the present method used to calculate interest on the balance due, as my hon. colleague just mentioned. Unfortunately, the current method is unfair and I think that the hon. member's bill is excellent in its approach to these issues in that credit card holders should pay interest on the balance due and not on the initial amount. I do not know whether the hon. member is aware of it; he talks about "double dipping". I can tell him about "triple dipping".
I personally met a restaurateur who accepts the American Express card. He told me that American Express does not pay restaurateurs immediately-a well-established procedure. My hon. colleague is mistaken if he thinks that everyone is compensated or paid right away when someone pays with a credit card. It can sometimes take 10 days, sometimes 21 days.
To conclude, I would like to mention that restaurateurs who accept the American Express card asked their customers to leave those cards at home. They did not exactly boycott them, but they would prefer their customers not to use them. So there is a serious problem of triple dipping.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I support the position taken by my hon. colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I entirely agree with his careful analysis of the matter before the House today-the interest rates charged by issuers of credit cards on balances due-and with his approach to dealing with this matter.
I am also aware of the concerns of the hon. member who introduced this private member's bill, and I fully support his goal, which is to help consumers who take advantage of the credit terms available to credit card users.
However, after considerable reflection, I must conclude that the proposal before us today is not very sensible and should not be adopted, in the circumstances.
Private Members' Business
I do not think we should make a decision without first giving full consideration to the needs of consumers and the consequences of measures that might be adopted by this House. We should pursue the ongoing process of regulatory reform launched by this government and not let ourselves be sidetracked by adopting special measures. The goal of our reforms is to ensure the stability of the financial sector and increase competition among the players in this industry, always in the interests of the consumer.
Both goals are necessary. If we undermine the stability of the financial sector, all sectors of our economy will suffer and automatically the consumer will be the loser.
Conversely, it is not in our interests to protect our financial institutions by reducing competition. Such a policy, were the government so rash as to implement it, would not only penalize the consumer but also hurt and weaken the competitive position of our financial industry-an industry that today is among the most advanced and most competitive in the world.
After these generalities about regulatory reform in the financial sector I would like to go on to the subject of credit card interest rates. There are several points I would like to make.
First of all, credit card interest rates and rates charged for the various types of credit available today are set by the market, which allows consumers to shop around for the best rate.
I may also point out that consumers with unpaid balances on their credit cards are usually in the higher income bracket and have a level of education that is higher than average. I would expect these people to have access to other, less costly forms of credit, such as a line of credit or a consumer loan, but we can only speculate on their reasons for deciding to use a more expensive form of credit.
One reason may be that they are not familiar with the various types of credits available. It is the role of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to make them aware of those possibilities. Another reason might be that some people prefer to make full use of the credit offered by these cards because it is so practical. In the final instance, it is up to every individual to weigh the pros and cons of this commodity.

December 2, 1991
Private Members' Business
Second, I would like to say a few words about the cost of the credit extended by the issuers of credit cards. Of the three components of the cost of credit, only one, the cost of borrowing money, has gone down in recent months. If I may digress slightly, I would like to remind the House that it played an important role, together with the present government and the Bank of Canada, in fighting inflation so that this drop in interest rates could occur. I think the hon. member who tabled the bill will agree.
The other components of credit costs-administration costs for credit card services and the cost of establishing reserves to cover bad debts-do not necessarily go down when interest rates go down. Although its purpose is not to cap interest rates, the bill before us this morning proposes to legislate the way interest is calculated on unpaid credit card balances. Consequently, it should be assessed according to the same criteria as any other rate setting measure.
Well intentioned though this measure may be, it asks Parliament to take unilateral action. So far, the various parties concerned by this matter have not been able to agree. I would therefore ask hon. members to analyse this question and discuss it at length before taking such concrete action.
In concluding, I believe that the best way to give consumers a chance to get the cheapest type of credit possible is to let the market decide. The financial sector legislation tabled by the government will expand the range of options offered to consumers. Thanks to such measures, which are the result of well prepared consultations and discussions with the various parties in our financial sectors, we will be better able to respond to the whole range of consumer needs.
I must therefore vote against this bill, and I recommend that we look for other ways to ensure that the financial sector's operations are sound and also fair to the consumer. Consequently I would also ask hon. members to vote against this proposal.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to have just listened to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance because, quite frankly, I think that the government had a rare
chance to do something here today that, contrary to what he would suggest, will not in any way, shape, or form upset the fiscal framework of the financial institutions in this country.
What the member for Mississauga South is doing in presenting this private member's bill is pleading for fairness and is pleading on behalf of all of the consumers in Canada. We know there are close to 50 million credit cards in circulation right now.
In an economy that is as depressed as our economy is at this moment in time and when our financial institutions are showing record breaking profit margins, it would seem to me that it would not only spur on some of the activity that we need so badly, but it would be a concrete action that this government could support. It would be an action that it really does believe in some kind of fairness in the economic system.
I can only say to the member, because it looks like the government is going to talk out this private member's bill, regretfully, as another member from a downtown Toronto market like the member for Mississauga South, we on this side are totally behind your bill. Maybe, in the not too distant future, the government will finally see the light on amending this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment the hon. member for Mississauga South on the the bill he has put before the House this morning, Bill C-237.
It is a bill which seeks to provide fairness to people using credit cards. The instance that comes to mind is a constituent who actually is a solicitor in my riding who acts on behalf of one of the chartered banks. He describes a couple of months ago when his bill for his credit card purchases over the month was something like $1,700.
He could not make out one of the charges, who it was from. It was charged to a numbered company. It was not the corporate name. He inquired. He paid the rest of the bill. I believe it was something like $1,650, but he did not pay the charge of $50. It turned out to be a restaurant charge, but instead of the name of the restaurant, it was a numbered company.

December 2, 1991

He sent in the bill for $1,650. He did not pay for the one charge of $50, and lo and behold the next month, he was charged interest on the entire $1,700 for the month. Needless to say, he was absolutely furious.
I do not know how the parliamentary secretary can stand up in the House today and make statements like: "You should not penalize the consumer". Surely the existing credit card interest rate law is penalizing the consumer. The banks' interest rates are too high anyway, but surely they should not be charging interest for payments that have been made as an extraordinary penalty.
The parliamentary secretary says that we should analyse the issue and then choose. The House has analysed the issue here this morning and has chosen to go with the member for Mississauga South.
The parliamentary secretary says that we should debate the issue. We have debated the issue. The parliamentary secretary really lost the debate. He did not put up good arguments.
I would hope that at some time, whether it is today or very near in the future, by unanimous consent and realistic thinking by the Minister of Finance and the parliamentary secretary, this bill could be brought back by unanimous consent and passed. It is the only fair way to treat consumers of this country.

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-20, an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament on February 26, 1991, as
Government Orders

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
These six motions are to delete clauses in the bill. There are six motions in amendment to Bill C-20, an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament on February 26, 1991, at report stage.

December 2, 1991
Government Orders
Motions Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 in the name of the hon. member for Essex-Windsor will be grouped for debate. A vote on Motion No. 1 will apply to Motion No. 2.
Motion No. 3 will be voted on separately and a vote on Motion No. 4 will apply to Motions Nos. 5 and 6.

Motion No. 1
That Bill C-20 be amended by deleting Clause 2.
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-20 be amended by deleting Clause 3.
Motion No. 3
That Bill C-20 be amended by deleting Clause 7.
Motion No. 4
That Bill C-20 be amended by deleting Clause 8.
Motion No. 5
That Bill C-20 be amended by deleting Clause 9.
Motion No. 6
That Bill C-20 be amended by deleting Clause 20.
He said: Mr. Speaker, what we have in front of us is the heart of the government cutbacks, commitments and expenditures which formed part of the budget put before this House back in the late winter. We have discussed this bill in committee and many groups came to testify before us. We are talking about a large number of groups, some of which appeared, some of which submitted briefs. There were approximately 25 to 30 groups. Every single one of them spoke out against this legislation.
These amendments attempt to pinpoint the specific areas of the legislation to which groups across this country and people across this country have objected most strongly.
The first two amendments would deal with the extension of the freeze on transfers to the provinces for health care and ior post-secondary education. I find it absolutely remarkable that a government can be proclaiming that it is working for greater prosperity, greater competitiveness in this country, a better education system, and at the same time putting before us clauses such as these two which will would cut back the amount of support available for post-secondary education.
I also have to say that the groups we heard from, with respect to health, represented an impressive array right
across the entire dimensions of the health community in this country. I have in front of me the brief which was presented by the Canadian Medical Association. The Canadian Medical Association is not a radical organization, it is not an organization which has any commitment except to see to it that there is a good health care system in this country. Its recommendation to us was that Bill C-20 be deferred until the results of the review of the tax collection agreements and the federal transfer discussions including the fiscal equalization program are known.
It also suggested to us that there should be legislation introduced to mandate federal support for health programs. It suggested that there has to be a serious look at how we are spending money in the health care field. It has to be done with urgency and it cannot be done if we have the kinds of cutbacks in this bill.
One of the most shocking pieces of evidence came out in the discussions with the Canadian Medical Association.
Here is an initiative from the federal government which will seriously impact the health system of this country. I can tell Canadians across this country this proposal was not even discussed with the medical doctors in this country. It was not discussed with nurses, it was not discussed with the various support staffs which make up our hospitals. It is especially scandalous that it was not even discussed with the medical association in this country.
We also suggest that section 7 dealing with the Public Utilities Income lax Transfer Act should be struck because this too freezes the amount of money which can be transferred to the provinces. The federal government is trying to offload on to the provinces the economic mess which it has made in terms of the deficit over the past seven and a half years.
Section 8 should also be deleted. It is the section which increases premiums for the Unemployment Insurance Act.
We feel that to put this extra tax into effect in the middle of a recession in this country is not just foolish economics, it is tragic for the people who are faced with increased payments at a time when they are already stretched to the limit. We hope that clause will be struck from this legislation.
December 2, 1991

We suggest that section 9 be struck, which also deals with the question of premiums under the UI act.
It has been a remarkable experience to listen to groups from across this country such as the B.C. Association of Community Care, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Canadian Co-Operative Association, the Canadian Federation of Labour, the Canadian Federation of Students, the Canadian Health Coalition, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Nurses Association, the Canadian Public Health Association, and one can continue through the list of the health care advocates of British Columbia.
Group after group came before us saying that something needed to be done about health care expenditure and that to tighten the noose around our health care system at this point is a serious threat to the future of medicare in this country.
Medicare is one of those things, perhaps the most important, which tie our country together and give our people a sense of pride and a sense of commitment to Canada. For us to even be thinking about these cutbacks, which will make it more difficult and some groups said impossible to improve our medical care system in Canada and make it work for the future, is a very sad step to take.
I hope this House will not take it. I hope these amendments will be accepted.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on these particular amendments.
I would like to take the opportunity to point out to the House that this is one of the most deceptive strategies I have seen used by the NDP in the promotion of health care. That is what it has chosen to do. If you look at the amendments, you will say to yourself: "What is left?" What is left is section 4, which is a Draconian attack on other social programs and education programs in this country. If you looked at the legislation and accepted their strategy, the only thing is that the federal government would do would be able to take money from other programs to protect health care. That sounds like a social good, we all want to protect health care, but this is where the Conservatives and the NDP agree. Instead of providing funds, instead of developing a fair tax strategy and instead of financing this government properly, what it will do is take from every other program in order to support medicare. This is very much reminiscent of the
Government Orders
strategies being tried by other parties, such as the British Labour Party, to focus people in on one program to scare them and, at the same time, make other groups feel very, very vulnerable.
For example, if you followed the NDP strategy on this one, people could lose money from equalization payments affecting post-secondary education. If you look at the brief, which was very carefully omitted in the review by the member for Essex-Windsor, there is a note from the Canadian Federation of Students who were absolutely astounded by the impact that this legislation was going to have on education. If you followed this strategy and these amendments as structured, these students would be made even more vulnerable because it says that the only thing left for the federal government to do to improve health care is to take money from students and from faculty.
This also was raised by the Canadian Association of University Teachers. It found this most Draconian. It can take away equalization payments which are estimated to be $8.4 billion; the financing of the Northwest Territories estimated to be $1.41 billion; grants in lieu of taxes from the municipalities estimated to be $344 million; public utilities income tax transfers estimated at $280 million; statutory subsidies estimated to be $36 million; the cost of income maintenance and social services under the Canada Assistance Plan, $6.4 billion; crop insurance contributions estimated to be $207 million; formula under official languages estimated at $243 million; miscellaneous health and welfare, $170 million; young offenders services, $158 million; justice transfers, $77 million; transportation transfers, $69 million.
This particular strategy, if you follow these amendments, is to side step the most difficult question which is how do you properly finance the health care system?
This government was honest in its strategy. It said: "We are going to cut back to the provinces and we are going to take money from other programs to protect health care". That is an honest strategy. The second strategy is: "Let us ignore what is really going on and let us show people that we are trying to protect medicare. Let us forget about the fact that we are going to take money from other programs. Let them find out after". A good example of this is the strategy being followed by the NDP Government of Ontario where it is taking money from the health care system and closing hospitals. It knows the reality. It has to face this reality. It is not living in a dream world which is reflected in these clauses.

Government Orders
A more direct strategy would be to deal with the legislation in its entirety, to understand that the whole concept is wrong and to vote against the entire bill. To pick and choose a clause such as this is perpetrating, I would dare say, a fraud upon the Canadian public because members will be able to pick out these little speeches and say: "We are really fighting for medicare". In fact, they are destroying medicare and it should be stopped right here.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the amendments.
One thing that is becoming very, very clear is that our national medicare program as we now know it in Canada is under attack. It has been under attack for a good number of years, starting in 1977 when the Liberals abandoned the concept of partnership with the federal government and the provinces and the 50/50 sharing of a national health care program.
They finally, in 1982-83, abandoned it further with the 6 and 5 program, when they curtailed the transfer payments to the provinces under EPF. They showed the Tories how they could attack the transfer payments on a systematic basis. Of course, the Tories learned very quickly.
One of things we have to look at is what is the implication for a national health care program. At this point in time in Canadian history, when there is a need and strong reasons for people wanting a national federal government, this government seems to be determined to ensure that in Canada, the national institution that people value most, which is our national medicare, is sacrificed.
It is the one thing that Canadians identify themselves with. When you ask a Canadian why they want to belong to Canada, one of the first things they will mention is our national medicare program.
What has this government done? It has started to erode the ability of the provinces to meet the five criteria set out in the Canada Health Act. The cutbacks that are now taking place that started in 1986, then went on to
Bill C-69 and are now envisioned in this bill, will amount to $62.4 billion by the year 2000.
People should clearly understand that these cutbacks are not based on an escalating cost. The federal government is not obligated to match the cost. It was based on the concept of the increase in the Gross Domestic Product.
In other words, the increase would only be there as the economy increased. Yet, it has said in order to meet our responsibilities for national health care, it is not willing to have this increase continue in spite of the fact there will be a growth in the economy. It simply said it will be zeroed, regardless of the expansion of the economy. This means that there is a $62.4 billion loss to the provinces.
In the final year, it will equal $10.9 billion in that year alone. My home province of British Columbia will have lost over $5 billion by the year 2000, nearly one-half billion dollars in this year alone.
The impact on the weaker provinces has already been devastating. Newfoundland had to lay off 10 percent of its nursing staff. Other provinces have had to cut-out pharmacare programs, dental health programs for children and have had to curtail preventive health majors.
The government will also be in a position with these cuts that it will no longer be in a position to enforce the Canada Health Act because there will be no transfer payments of cash to the provinces, for some provinces as early as 1997 and for all provinces by the year 2004. That means the federal government will no longer be able to enforce their standards.
It has brought in what it thinks is a solution and that is to attach moneys to other programs. We did not even bother to make an amendment to delete it. That section is so odious we even are assured that the Tory backbenchers will rise up and defeat that section. There is no need to make an amendment to delete it. There is not even a Tory in this country who will stand up in this House and say: "In order to enforce accessibility to health care, we are going to take money from starving children under the Canada Assistance Plan".

The Liberals thought of it.
December 2, 1991

Yes, the Liberals thought of it. Not even the Tories will have the nerve to stand up in this House and support that they are going to take money from child abuse, investigation and protection of children in child abuse situations, to enforce a standard of accessibility. We do not feel this amendment is necessary as we are quite confident even the Tories will not have the nerve to stand in this House and pass section 4 of this act.
There is no way in this political climate in Canada that the question of federal spending powers is paramount and the ability to direct social programs on a national basis, or that the federal government is going to be allowed to either attach Canada Assistance Plan payments or equalization payments to enforce federal legislation into which it is no longer putting money.
There have been many legal opinions that simply say that section is unconstitutional, do not worry about it, it will never stand a constitutional test. Those constitutional tests are being readied.
With regard to this piece of legislation, I, like my colleague, sat in on many of the committee hearings. Group after group, as diverse as professional groups to community advocacy groups, appeared before that committee and every single one of them condemned this legislation. They condemned it because it is a betrayal of our national institution of medicare. They condemned it because the federal government's only solution to mismanaging the economy and the debt is to off-load that debt on to the provinces and to the provincial health care systems.
It has not saved any money by doing that. In fact, it has jeopardized the provinces' ability to take some innovative approaches to containing health care costs. The innovative approaches are there at the provincial level. All you have to do is look at the reports that have been done by a number of provinces, including the Seaton report done in British Columbia.
The provinces know that there must be certain areas of change within their health care administration. They are willing to make them, to put more emphasis on non-institutional care; to put more emphasis on prevention; to put more emphasis on support. However, they can only
Government Orders
do so if they have dollars. This bill is designed to strangle the very foundation of our national medicare system and regrettably I think with it to strangle Canada as we now know it.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe my ears this morning, that the New Democratic Party, rather than facing this debate head on is trying to set up a diversion. The member talked about all the various people that came to the finance committee to oppose Bill C-20. I found it interesting this morning and I stand to be corrected if he did mention this group, but I did not hear him mention earlier Dr. Michael Rachlis. He made his presentation to the Standing Committee on Finance, opposing Bill C-20 and the fact that it was probably not constitutional. The member failed to mention that, and Dr. Rachlis quite prominently declares that he is a member of the New Democratic Party. He also happens to be a constituent of mine. He has written a book, Second Opinion: What's Wrong with Canada's Health Care System, where he talks about the difficulties with the health care system in Canada. He wrote this book with Ms. Carol Kushner.
What I do not understand from the New Democratic Party is that it does not talk about the thrust of Rachlis where he says that there are some solutions if we would face this problem head on. Instead, the New Democratic Party wants to set up this diversion system where we start toying with taking funding from other programs. I do not think Canadians want us to rob Peter to pay Paul. If we are going to talk in this House about national standards of education, training and retraining, why set up a series of amendments where in order to look after the medical system of this country we are going to take away from the educational system. I think my colleague for Winnipeg North Centre was correct in saying that we are going to oppose these amendments. Hopefully we will have a solid, constructive and creative debate today opposing the government's Bill C-20. I hope in the process of debate we can come up with some ideas of where we can preserve and maintain the standards of our national health care system without bringing in all kinds of diversions.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take a brief part in this debate. After listening to the two speakers from the Official Opposition I was hard put not to break into tears or throw up.

December 2, 1991
Government Orders
I am reminded of a famous time in the British Parliament in 1945 when Mr. Churchill brought in legislation to extend rationing of coal and fish. Aneurin Bevan, who is one of my political heroes and a famous democratic socialist from Wales by the way, stood up and said: "Mr. Speaker, England is an island of coal surrounded by a sea of fish and only the organizational genius of the right hon. gentleman could see to it that we had a shortage of both".
Canada is a nation that has the resources, the talents and the gifted people to raise the money and finance fully these various programs affected by this legislation. But only the organizational genius of this Tory government could see to it that they are reduced and undermined. We are trying to stop that.
The first speaker from the Official Opposition criticized us because there is one clause that my colleague, our spokesman on this bill, did not move to delete. That is the one to provide penalties to the provinces if they do not abide by the five principles of medicare. We happen to think that when a province tries to undermine any one or more of those five principles, it should be penalized. It should be penalized because there goes universality and there goes comprehensive coverage.
I find it appalling to see any Liberal or any Tory get up and talk about how much they support and are in favour of medicare. The gall and the nerve of them.
I was in Saskatchewan in 1962 when the Liberals and the Tories organized the opposition to the implementation of medicare in that province. They brought out thousands of people in front of the legislative buildings to oppose it. The doctors supported them and the opposing of the implementation of medicare in that province. They wanted to govern according to who could get the largest mob out even though the governmeBnt of the day was elected with a majority and the number one program was the instituting of medical care. I get sick to my stomach when I have to put up with listening to Grits and Tories who have made great talk about how they support medicare.
It was the Liberals in 1975 under the then Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, who started it. They have the gall to get up and talk about
how they are going to fight this bill and oppose it. They never have believed in it. They never have worked for it or supported it.
The same thing applies to the Conservative government. They are the same breed of cats. There is not any difference. The only difference is one is in and one is out. We have had nothing but the same nonsense.
Liberals tell me how they brought in national medicare in 1966. Do you know why, Mr. Speaker? In 1963 and 1965 there were minority Parliaments. It was people like Tommy Douglas and Stanley Knowles who said to the government: "You bring this in or we'll defeat you". They had to be dragged kicking and screaming into the 20th century.
They have convenient memories. They do not like to remember or be reminded. It does not matter which one is in. You have to force them into doing what is decent and civilized and yes even Christian.
I do not understand why any government would have the gall to bring in the cutbacks that are occurring. The Established Programs Financing Act in itself is governed by the fact that the provinces do not get an increase unless their population increases. Under the organizational genius of federal and provincial Tory governments in my province we have had a net outflow of people. Saskatchewan does not need this part of the bill because we are already going to get a reduction because we have had a reduction in population.
I was going to talk about have not provinces but nowadays all the provinces are have not. Ones that were looked upon as wealthy and which contributed the most money to equalization programs are in real trouble. The whole country is in the same boat.
The solution this government has is equivalent to R. B. Bennett of 1935 and then Mackenzie King right up until the declaration of war which is cut back and reduce. One Minister of Finance said to T. C. Douglas the then member for Weyburn: "The hon. member must think that money grows on gooseberry bushes". Within a week after the declaration of war the Liberal government of that day found the bush. There was lots of money. All of a sudden we were rolling in it to do anything and everything that needed to be done to prosecute a war. If any war was ever justified that one was.
December 2, 1991

If you were to take the national debt at the end of the Second World War and translate it into 1991 dollars it would be greater than the one we have now. If you took the deficit at the last fiscal year during the Second World War and translated it into 1991 dollars it would be equal to if not greater than the present one.
But we paid it off.

You're damn right we paid it off. Following the war we had to rebuild our entire economy. Our manufacturing plants and our municipal infrastructure all had to be rebuilt. All had gone through the dirty thirties and the wartime and little could had been put into them. We had full employment. When you have full employment people pay taxes. Within 10 years all those debts were paid off. Without a full employment policy no party or government can really do anything about our annual deficit and our debt.
There is so much that has to be done and needs to be done in this country. It hits you in the face every time you go back to your own constituency and your own province. There are scores of cities and large towns in this country that have a waiting list as long your arm for chronic care beds, senior citizen housing, low income co-op housing, sewer and water systems that are worn out and raw sewage that runs into our lakes and rivers. It all needs to be fixed. It means hundreds of thousands of jobs. A quarter of a million people could be put to work over the next 10 years just to clean up our air and our water.
The governments we have had since 1867 do not know what to do or how to do it. They have neither the courage nor the interest to do it because it is not in the interests of the corporations who support and finance them. I invite my hon. friends to read a little book called The Unnecessary Evil, not written by an NDPer but by Professor Rubin Ballen of the University of Manitoba. I invite members to read it. He throws into a cocked hat all the nonsense we have been getting ad nauseam about debt and deficits.
The cutting back that is going on now and that started with the Liberals in 1975 has been self-defeating because unemployment got worse and the debt got worse. He showed that up for the kind of nonsense it is.
I want to compliment my colleague for his amendments. They do what we think needs to be done with this
Government Orders
legislation unless the government has the courage of its convictions and withdraws the whole damned thing.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make some comments about the amendments that have been put forward. I take particular umbrage at my colleague for Regina- Lumsden who many times debates strongly in this House and did so just a few weeks ago dealing with the merchant mariners. It was an action I supported.
I cannot sit here and allow the NDP version of history to go into Hansard unchallenged. There are times in this House where you either sit back and laugh or you stand up and put your position clearly on the record. It galls me a little bit too much whenever I hear the self-righteous group to my left over here-they are truly to my left-getting up and trying to rewrite history. My goodness if we listened to the member for Regina-Lumsden, they were responsible for the sun shining in this place since the New Democratic Party was formed and prior to that CCF.
I have a great deal of respect for the CCF part and their traditions. I have a great deal of respect for some of the statesmen that party has produced like Tommy Douglas and Stanley Knowles who sits at this table as an honorary officer. But I take a great deal of umbrage at the hon. member trying to take credit for every single good measure that was put in by people like Lester B. Pearson, a Liberal Prime Minister and the protections that were given to health care in this country by the ministers and the government of Pierre-Elliott Trudeau.
When were they in office?

One of my colleagues asks: "When were they in office?" They have not been in office. I am not illiterate. I read as much as I can about the history of this place and the history of the various political philosophies and how they unfold. If you listen to the New Democratic Party this Parliament must have been shuddering.
It must have been just shaking in its boots during that period when health care, medicare, came in here. It must have been waiting for the New Democratic Party over here to the left to come in and bang the desk and say: "Let's do this or otherwise you are going to be out of this place". Absolute nonsense.

December 2, 1991
Government Orders
It is absolute nonsense to take away the contribution of people like Pierre-Elliott Trudeau, Lester B. Pearson or Allan J. MacEachen who were the social conscience of this place and who were responsible for more socially progressive legislation than almost anybody who sat in this place. Monique Begin stood against the provinces that were coming forward with user fees. The hon. member was here during that period.
If the member wants to get up and speak on the amendments and on the regressive nature of this bill, so be it. He has a responsibility and a right to do it. I also have a right to get up and put the record straight.
Anybody who reads the history of this place knows what I am saying is correct. It appears that it is fine for the hon. member to get up on his hind feet and to bay at the moon whenever a bill comes in here. Those members want to take credit for anything that was done by the Liberal Party.
He also has to understand that there have been certain actions taken by colleagues who wear his own cloth, his New Democratic colleagues, particularly in the province of Ontario, like Mr. Bob Rae, "Mr. Cut-cut". He comes in with a promise that everything is going to be fine in la-la land. He was going to pave every street and there were going to be two chickens in every pot. The New Democrats can do that.
What do they do? They come into the province of Ontario in a fluke. It was an absolute fluke that the people of Ontario elected a majority of New Democrats to the government. It was 37 per cent or 38 per cent who came forward and voted for the New Democrats. By luck they got in and it has been nothing but downhill since in Ontario.
I come from a part of Canada that has been a have not part of Canada for a long time. I am going to tell you right now, I think I would rather live in Nova Scotia than in Ontario led by Bob Rae and the New Democrats. There is a hospital a day closing. They are merging them, they are shutting beds down, they are denying help to those who need help the most in the province of Ontario.
Yet the New Democratic Party gets up here and wants to say: "Look, what we are going to have to do is to set the record straight. If medicare is good, we will take the credit for it. If UIC is good, we will take the credit for it".
Parliament must be changed because I am in this place and I certainly feel that I can get up and articulate my position on any issue I want. I look across here and we are always trying to advise the government about better ways to come forward with legislative programs. Sometimes it listens but most times it does not. It must have been a different place back in 1966 when medicare came in. We must have all had an NDP guardian angel sitting on our shoulder who used to whisper sweet nothings in our ears the night before. Then we would come in, do all that was right and just and the NDP would take the credit for it.
My hon. colleague, the minister opposite, said he was here at that point. He assures me that the New Democrats were not angels. I will leave it to my hon. colleague to explain what they were at that point.
Let us set the record straight. These particular amendments do not address the substance or the intent of the bill. It is fine to say take this away or do that. We are in favour of preserving medicare, and that is a very noble endeavour.
We fought for that since we introduced it and passed it in this place as Liberals in 1966. We will continue to fight for that.
To talk about making the poor poorer and giving the government the ability to walk in and start tampering with some other transfers for social programs which are equally as important to those individuals who have to rely on those transfers is irresponsible in my view.
It is fine for the member opposite from the New Democratic Party to come in here and to rewrite history in the 20 brief minutes he had. I would hope that anybody who is watching this debate will look at the substance of the bill. The bill is bad. The amendments put forward by the New Democratic Party are equally as bad because they ring hollow when put up to public scrutiny.
As for the explanations given by my hon. colleague who has delivered some masterful speeches on the right issues in this House and who has had my support on those occasions, even his fancy rhetoric cannot give depth and body to the shallow amendments that have been put forward by his colleague.
December 2, 1991

Mr. Speaker, it has been an interesting history lesson for the last 20 minutes from a variety of perspectives. I would like to comment on the speech of my colleague from Regina-Lumsden who has put it into the proper perspective.
I remember being a very young person at the time when medicare came in to Saskatchewan and if it had not been for the political courage of people like Tommy Douglas, this country would still not have a medicare program, and that is a fact.
The member for Dartmouth has just gone on about people baying at the moon. I think he should look in the mirror to get a good example of what baying at the moon is all about.
Medicare in Canada is something that all Canadians treasure. They see it as being uniquely Canadian, something they have worked and struggled for over a long period of time. During the depression many people were without medical care. My mother-in-law, who was a young girl in Saskatchewan then, had appendicitis and her family could not afford a doctor. If it had not been for her older brother picking her up and saying to her mother and father "she's got to get to the hospital", she would not be alive today because the appendix had broken. The situation for ordinary people at that time was that you simply could not go to a doctor because it was a choice between feeding your family or finding medical care. They left it too long. It was not a situation of not caring, it was a situation of not being able.
That has changed in Canada today. People can go to hospitals and can attend doctors, and we cannot see that eroded by the successive Liberal and Conservative governments.
We see delegations coming up to Canada from the United States over and over again to examine our medicare system. There is a bigger movement in the United States now asking for a medical system in the United States similar to the situation in Canada. What those delegations have discovered and what Canadians have discovered through those delegations is that our system of a national medicare program is far more cost effective than the system of private medical care in the United States. Not only is it fairer and not only do people have access to medical care, but it is more cost
Government Orders
effective than the system in the United States. It saves money, it does not cost more money.
What have we seen in the last several years? In 1977, first of all, it was the Liberals who changed the cost sharing mechanism for medicare and EPF. They changed it from the 50:50 financing between the federal government and the provincial governments. That was the first step at eroding national medical care, and we can thank the Liberals for that.
After that Mulroney came to power in 1984 and what did he promise? He promised then to maintain transfer payments. He talked about a sacred trust for Canadians on social programs. In 1986 this government, the Conservative government, started its attack on EPF funding and medicare and post-secondary education.
In 1990 the Conservatives brought in Bill C-69 which froze the entitlements at the EPF levels of 1989 until 1992. Now we have Bill C-20 which extends that until 1994 or 1995.
These EPF cuts endanger our health care system and they endanger our post-secondary education system.
The impact on the country is huge. A freeze to the EPF, this bill, means a loss of over $97 billion by the year 2000. These are not little bits of money we are talking about, these are massive cuts in programs that Canadians have come to treasure.
What do the messages in this bill bring to Canadians who are waiting for hospital beds? In my province of British Columbia we have long waiting lists for hospital beds. We have a situation in which people who are waiting for heart operations are forced to go down to Seattle because there is not enough operating room time to take care of our own people.
These cuts, combined with the other Draconian policies of the Conservative government, mean a loss of over $5 billion to British Columbia by the year 2000. We are already in a critical health care situation. We already have people lined up. I get more letters from constituents who are concerned and angry because one of their family members cannot get into a hospital to get the required surgery with these waits and these line-ups. This is only going to get worse with the cutbacks and freezing of transfer payments.

Government Orders
This bill is actually a direct threat to the national standards as they are set out under the Canada Health Act. The people who are most affected by the cuts of the Conservative government, and this bill is just another example of that ongoing mania of cut, cut, cut, are women and children.
A subcommittee of the House of Commons is having hearings on the increased incidence of breast cancer for Canadian women and women in North America, the whole issue of reproductive health care for women, the whole issue of health care for children, and on Canada with over a million children living in poverty. These cuts are a further erosion of the services that women and children need from our society. This is opening the door for over-billing, for fee for services, for cutting services, for transferring insurance to private insurance, for creating in our country a two-tiered health system.
Women and children are always the hardest hit when health care becomes inaccessible. Single mothers and children make up the majority of lower income families. This government goes on with its tax giveaways to big business while all the time turning its back on people who need help most. It is turning its back on children who are living in poverty and children who are lining up at food banks for a basket of groceries with their mothers. The low income citizens and the middle class are always the ones who bear the brunt of Conservative policies.
This bill also attacks our post-secondary education system at a time when under-funding is already crippling Canadian universities. How can this government talk ad nauseam about economic growth, competition, competing in the world market on one hand while continuing to weaken the very institutions which can provide the training and technology that the people of Canada need in order to compete in the world markets? How can it continue to talk about equality for women while it reduces women's access to quality education?
Education will give women the opportunity they need to get into higher paying jobs and help to break the cycle of poverty for women. Women in this country still earn only 66 per cent of what men do for full-time, full-year work. This government is again slamming the door on women and slamming the door on young people, Canadians who will not be able to afford a university education.
My colleague from Regina said earlier that in the late 1930s when money was needed it was found to fight a war. The same thing happened in this House a year ago. Now we hear that there are no funds for child care, we hear that there are no funds for health care, none for social services. Money was found to fight the gulf war.
