Mr. Speaker, I wanted to join in this debate today because as we were planning it we thought it was significant that there be a major discussion about what will be, without question, a turning point in the history of this country.
The turning point is simply that the federal government is dramatically altering the role it plays in a variety of programs it shares with the provinces such as education, health care, housing and social programming. New ideas are just beginning to get developed around care for children and around issues that perhaps were not talked about a decade ago such as child abuse and the abuse of women.
Now we are just beginning to identify the problem and starting to put in place some programs that will rectify that. We all admit that they are the last programs in and so they will struggle for funding under normal times. This bill puts a beach head in place which says we should not count on the federal government to carry its fair share any more. It has abandoned that.
As I watched the debate, the first thing that struck me as being odd is why there are no Conservative members standing up to defend the cause. Then the answer became apparent. They did not need to. Their traditional allies are standing up defending their cause.
At one time it used to be said that Liberals were Tories in a hurry. These days, that is wrong. These days Tories are Liberals in a hurry. Where Pierre-Elliott Trudeau only wanted a six and five mandatory wage restraint program across the country, the Tories are not satisfied with that kind of peanuts, they want zero, absolutely nothing.

I recall being a health critic for the provincial party in the late seventies. The person with whom I argued at that time was a Liberal, Monique Begin, a very fine person, but she put in place the Established Programs Financing system, block funding and a number of other variations to the traditional means whereby the federal government shared its costs with the provinces.
At that time in each of the provinces there was not an outcry but a warning that this would make it easy for the federal government to begin to retreat from its obligations. I recall at the time she said: "No, we would never do that" and then promptly proceeded to do just exactly that.
I recall at the time people were saying: "This is going to make it very difficult to get new programs in place because while we struggle with a restraint package from Ottawa, we have to kind of work with an existing system".
There has been a lot of discussion here today about the health care system in Canada. It is perhaps one of the foremost in the world. It is far from being a perfect system however. It struggles to adjust to new conditions, not just new funding, but new technology, new ideas and new concepts. That is understandable because people who are dominating the health care system in this country are trained in very traditional ways and have probably worked a long time to establish the kind of programs for health care that they know about and are familiar with.
When someone comes along and suggests to them that perhaps traditional care in a hospital bed is not the only way to provide care, they listen to those arguments with great caution. They are not terribly receptive to them. I would say it is reasonable to judge their performance as being cautiously accepting that as true, that perhaps there are community health centres that could do it in a more cost efficient way, but they are very cautious people.
To get them to change from one type of provision of care to another is going to take a little while, a little pushing and shoving and a little convincing. I think that process is under way.
The tragedy though is simply this: to accept what is in this bill, to accept what the Liberals and the Tories are so valiantly supporting this morning, is to accept that no new ideas will ever make their way to the forefront. It
Government Orders
means wrecking one system to try to put in place another without providing any kind of transition.
That I think goes across the board no matter what kind of care you are trying to provide. If you are trying to provide some different kind of care for people who run afoul of the law and you do not like the prisons, which none of us do, and you do not like the traditional punishment approach, which none of us do, and you want to try something else, how do you get the something else in place? How do you provide the new model for providing care and counselling and treatment in place?
The truth is in all of our ridings. These things are happening but they are struggling. While many of us were happy to see an old prison system virtually taken apart, I think all of us would be equally unhappy at the moment that we do not have the reasonable financing in place to provide some alternative to that. We are stuck between the two.
Many of us are advocates of a great many things that have to do with the needs of women in a modern day society, providing child care, providing proper housing, providing some kind of counselling, providing some kind of retraining. All of us will be familiar that in our communities these ideas are just getting started.
I would not be thrilled with a government that said it is putting on the brakes to everything it has ever done in terms of traditionally providing health care for the very young or the very old. I would not be happy if it said it was stopping dead in the water on that and it was going to channel some money into new ideas. I do not think it can work that way. I believe that what we need is a sensible, rational and logical transition from one type of providing care to people to something that might look quite different.
In the end the different type of care might be more cost effective. In my view that is not the argument. The argument ought to be whether it is better care. It will be incidental that it will be done with fewer tax dollars.
The final argument that I want to make this morning is one of perception. I admit that right off the bat. Maybe it has not much to do with the reality of how you divide up the tax dollar. But it is incredibly frustrating for Canadian citizens in their own homes to read about a government preaching restraint that paid $104,000 to transport one person from Senegal back to Ottawa.

December 2, 1991
Government Orders
It is real tough for people in my riding who will not get an increase in whatever their benefits are this year and who struggle for the kind of programs that they desperately need to know that the Minister of National Revenue spent $10,000 to go and talk to the Rotary Club in Hamilton.
We think it is fine that he goes and talks to them. We think it is fine to provide adequate transportation for the minister to go back to Saskatchewan at $35,000 a crack. What we are struggling with is simply the notion of how in the world we can talk of spending that kind of money in one breath and talk about restraint for everybody else with the next.
If we saw you on the trains we would say it was great but that you probably should not be riding the trains all the time because you are tired. If we provide you with money to take commercial aircraft we would probably say it was all right. We understand you work hard and are tired and you need a break. Travel is a difficult part of political life.
What people do not understand and cannot fathom is how you can blithely go on spending money like that and preach restraint to them at the same time. In my riding this happens every single day. Someone walks in with an example of how government spends its money and then says that you have to be restrained in how you are provided with services.
That is what is wrong with this country. That is what these amendments attempt to propose. The debate has been interesting to say the least.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks about this bill. I would like to start by saying that I have experienced over the last couple of years my own husband being in and out of hospitals suffering from cancer. I cannot say too strongly how very important, valuable and cherished our Canadian health system is. This is despite the fact that this government and the previous Liberal government incidentally have continuously eroded the cost of federal funding. This in turn has caused provinces to cut back and take measures such as user fees and so on which are contrary to the Canada Health Act.
From personal experience it is wonderful to know that when you are under stress that you do have a secure health system and that there are not going to be a lot of bureaucratic hassles and worry about paying bills and cuts in services that are absolutely essential.
On the other hand I can also say from personal experience that it is deplorable to know that at this time certainly in British Columbia, and I am quite sure it is the same throughout Canada, there are wards of beds that are empty because hospitals cannot afford to finance adequate services to use the facilities to capacity. There are wonderful health care workers, including nurses and others, who continue to provide highly professional caring and services. I certainly commend them.
On the other hand they are overworked. There is no question about that. There is not enough staff. There is the whole question of para-professionals which in our provinces have been cut back. They have a significant impact on the extent and nature of the services.
As my colleague from New Westminster said, there are long waits for operations and for specialized services that are needed. In British Columbia we are also very concerned about the new commission appointed by the previous government. Interestingly enough, it recently came out with a report advocating some very positive reforms in health care services such as the kind of delivery services where we should be giving much greater emphasis to community based services and to prevention. It also advocates home care support so that institutional services which are often not as personalized and that are certainly more expensive will not be used to the same degree.
There are many reforms needed but we must have the finances to maintain and replace services that have been cut and to consider new kinds of community support services.
What is this government doing? There is no question that this government, which has cut back I believe four times in health care financing, has taken over $42 billion from Canada's health care services. This includes the cuts that will be forthcoming if this bill passes. Forty-two billion dollars will be taken from Canadian health care services.
I wonder how that will impact on the services for your family and mine and for Canadians across the country. It will have a devastating impact. I notice in some of the notes I have here also that we asked for the comments of the present minister of health. I will quote from a comment that was made on May 28, 1991 when he was being questioned about user fees as far as medicare is concerned. This was in relation to Quebec's plan to introduce a user fee for emergency ward services. He responded at that time as follows:

If you charge a user fee I fear that poor people will not go for the
service because they will fear having to pay money. I will never accept
two health systems; one for the poor and one for the rich.
That is a risk that is happening and he is absolutely right. The Minister of National Health and Welfare goes on to say: "If there is anything against the law I will act".
I would think this minister then should be acting very strongly to oppose this present bill which will cut the EPF funding for health care services and also for post-secondary education which is another very serious concern.
He should be the first one up on his feet saying that he does not support this bill. It is a very sneaky way of cutting back on funding because it means that health care services are eroded over a five-year period so that in effect EPF funding is removed altogether.
A brief from the Canadian Nurses Association to the Standing Committee on Finance stated that Bill C-20 represents the fourth successive attempt by the government to limit the federal role in medicare. It says that the cumulative effect of these changes is set out in a table which it provided and which shows that $42 billion will be taken from health care services by 1992 by the Conservative government.
We know also that the previous Liberal government said today how strongly they support medicare. I have a great deal of respect for the previous minister Monique Begin. But even Monique Begin when she was minister allowed block funding and the bills that established EPF funding to go through. Of course she found later that she had to defend very strongly the federal position and put some limits on provincial funding until they would adhere to the terms of the Canada Health Act.
I would like to remind people that the Canada Health Act which Canadians are so proud of is a goal that many Americans would love to see for their country. It established five principles for health care and they have worked well in this country. We have one of the best health care services in the world. We also have one of the most economically feasible health care systems.
Those five principles were universality, accessibility, comprehensiveness, public administration and portability so that we would not have a different kind of health service in different provinces as a person moves from one province to another. These are very sound principles that have been put to the test over the years since the Health Care Act was first introduced.
It is a tragedy and I hope that Canadians will realize that Bill C-20 and the kind of bills that were passed last year which eroded health care funding are eroding the basic Canada Health Act. It will be literally impossible for provincial governments to maintain universality, accessibility, portability, comprehensiveness and public administration in the way that it was intended under this act if they do not have the financing from the federal government to assist in doing this.
We have seen provincial governments bringing in user fees and using other means to cut back on access to health care partly because they do not have adequate funding.
I would like to mention some of the points that were raised at the finance committee by the health care advocates of British Columbia and I commend them for the brief to that committee. It is an excellent review of the evolution and the devolution of health care services in Canada. They point out that the principles of Canadian medicare as set out in the Canada Health Act must be preserved.
The Conservative government has deepened these cuts to the point where federal cash transfers for medicare and post-secondary education will end in a few years. These are not just cutbacks. It likes the public to think it is just cutbacks because of the deficit situation. Of course the Conservative love to blame social programs for that deficit.
The public needs to know that it is not just cutbacks. It is the actual demise of medicare and of post-secondary education funding as we know it over the next five years.

December 2, 1991
Government Orders
The health care advocates of British Columbia go on to say that the federal government passed the Medicare Act in 1966 under which it had agreed to fund half the cost of the provincial medicare insurance plans. Within six years every province had set up a plan that met these national standards. It is so important to maintain the national standards under our constitutional reforms that they are being debated as well. We must make sure these are maintained in our future programs.
Medicare has not only been one of the most important social programs in Canada, it is a point of pride and it is what makes us different as Canadians. It makes us proud to be Canadians and it brings unity to this country, a unity that is being eroded by this veiy bill. I know Canadians do not want that.
We are proud that our health care is the best in the world. In contrast the United States has more than 30 million people who lack health care. In Canada we have health insurance coverage for everyone. Some people will say it is too expensive. On the other hand if we look at the facts 9 per cent of Canada's gross domestic product is accounted for by health care whereas nearly 12 percent of the GDP in the United States is taken up by health care.
It is economically very fair. We must vote down this bill. My colleague had presented amendments in order to tiy alleviate the impact of this bill. It is a deplorable situation. I wish I had time to elaborate on the post-secondary education.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to enter into the debate today even for a short time on this very important legislation.
The government is slowly chipping away at the health and post-secondary education system that we set up in this country. It is chipping away at it and it is doing it, as my colleague from Vancouver East said, in a very sneaky way.
Do you know why? Let us take a look at what six pages of legislation are going to do. They are six pages in a bill called C-20, an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament on February 26, 1991. Unfortunately these six pages sum up what this government is doing to health and post-secondary education in Canada. It should be ashamed of itself for bringing this kind of legislation into the House.
I appreciate that members of the New Democratic Party are here today debating this bill and defending one of the cornerstones of what makes Canada what it is. One of the pillars which make Canada such an important and wonderful place to live is the health care system we have developed here.
To members on the opposite side who are critical of medicare and what it means, I suggest they go down to the United States and tear up their medicare card. I dare them to do that. They know that they will not do that. We have to defend medicare against this government and other parties that are doing their best to destroy the health care system.
There are a couple of other points that are important about what this government has done and what it is carrying on with. Under the Liberals in 1977 the system was changed from a system which basically tagged and identified the transfer of funds from the federal government to the provinces in the areas of post-secondary education and health to what is referred to as block funding. Provinces can basically spend the money on whatever priorities they see fit.
Allegations have been made that a number of provinces use federal health and post-secondary funding to pave highways and what have you. It is alleged that the previous government in British Columbia, the cousins of the government members here, used some of those funds at that time to finance boondoggles like the Coquihalla and other aspects like that.
To try and clarify that I asked the Secretary of State during a debate in the House if he could tell this House and give assurances to Canadians that when the federal government did transfer the federal funds for health and education, those funds were spent on health and education. The Secretary of State of the day said that we would have trust him that that was the case.
If the Canadian public, the taxpayers, knew that the Government of Canada transfers to the provinces some billions of dollars, and yet the minister responsible for that could not tell this House for sure that the money was being spent on health and education, I think taxpayers of this country would demand accountability from this Parliament. They would demand that we be able to tell them what we are going to do.
December 2, 1991

That changed from 1977 under the Liberals when they brought in block funding. I suggest that the Parliament of Canada should return to a system of a 50/50 funding basis, equal partners in the delivery of health and post-secondary education in Canada.
I think there is an obligation on the part of the Government of Canada to explain and to account to Canadian taxpayers for where that money is going. Usually, the argument we have from the federal government is: "Well, we do not get enough publicity out of it. We do not get to put our four by eight signs up".
I say that it is its own fault if the government cannot get enough publicity out of the money it spends on post-secondary education and health in the provinces. If you look at the statistics from my own province where transfer payments are going down and in which the former government was leading a fight against this government, you can see the impact that the federal role has. I accuse this government of not having the brains to try and explain to Canadians just what kind of federal involvement there can be. What we are seeing is the reverse. This government is making every effort it can to see that our health care system and post-secondary education system do not get the assistance and help they need.
We all have personal experiences concerning our contact with the health care system. I have had it this year and have gained some understanding of what it means when a member of your family has to use our health care system. In one particular case in my family the system reached the point at which this member has to go to Seattle now for health care. It is incredible that my father would have to go to Seattle to get cancer treatment because there is not room or enough facilities for him in Canada.
The members opposite sit here and heckle and talk about how they are not destroying health care. I dare you to say that to my father in Seattle today. I dare you to say that, because that is what is happening under right wing governments like this Conservative administration and like the Socred administration. Hopefully the new governments that have been elected across this country
Government Orders
provincially, and especially in British Columbia, will result in a revolution in health care in which we can develop health care standards that are necessary to ensure that Canadian citizens continue to receive the medical treatment they need.

Mr. Speaker,
I rise today to speak on this bill. A lot has been said about the health care and the post-secondary education clauses in this bill, but not a lot has been said about clauses 8, 9 and 10 in the section of this bill that addresses the increase in the UI premiums. I know a lot of people think this is a fait accompli, that no more discussion should be undertaken and nothing should be said about it.
I notice a lot of government members are throwing remarks across the floor. They are not obscene remarks, they are taken in good nature, but I do not see any of the members rising to make any public statements on any of these clauses or on any of our arguments. Why do they not get up and say something if they have something to say? They just sit there and would rather just ramble on.
The increase in unemployment insurance rates is something that is severely affecting all of the country. We see the number of lay-offs, the number of bankruptcies, the number of people who are just being put out of work and the number of companies and grocery stores that are closing because they just cannot take any more taxation. We see increases with the GST and now with this 7.1 per cent increase in UI premiums it means that more people are going to be laid off.
What is the effect? There are so many people out of work now that the unemployment insurance system cannot keep up. Last year in June we saw an increase of 24 per cent in UI premiums. The then Minister of Finance said that the government would meet any shortfall the system may have, but not six months later we saw a 24 per cent increase. Now we see another increase of 7.1 per cent which is going to take effect this year.
The original Unemployment Insurance Act, section
48.1	reads: "Notwithstanding section 48 the rate of premiums that persons employed in insurable employment are required to pay on each of 1990, 1991 and 1992 is 2.25 per cent of insurable earnings in that year".

December 2, 1991
Government Orders
We heard, as I mentioned, the Minister of Finance say that the government would make up any shortfalls that may occur. Then we saw a few months later a 24 per cent increase. That was in June.
Now it is December and we see an increase. Why are there these continuous increases? It is because more and more people are being put out of work, so more and more people are collecting UI benefits. Fewer and fewer people are paying into it.
It is a vicious circle. We are never going to catch up unless we come up with a plan, a program, that is going to create employment. That is the answer: full employment. Then the UI system will not have to be subsidized by anyone.
The way we are going now, we see more and more people being laid off. We see more and more people collecting UI. It is never going to end.
The amendment which is being proposed by my colleague from Essex-Windsor is one that will rectify a wrong. It will force the government to abide by the statement that was made by the finance minister that day when he said the government would make up any shortfalls.
We cannot allow this to continue. Regarding the government's economic policies and its fiscal restraint policies, it is telling everyone else that they have to cut back and it does not. The government wants to pull back any funding that it puts into any program and it wants to wash its hands of everything and it wants the taxpayers to take up the slack that its failure is causing.
We need fiscal responsibility and it has to start on that side of the House. We need a government that is going to show some confidence in this country because there is no more confidence in this country. The morale in Canada is so low that everyone wants to move away. Where are they going to go? Where are they going to go to work? There is a grocery chain in Timmins, a local company which has been there for 30 years, which just announced last week that it is closing. It is closing right down completely.
The food banks are growing. There is something wrong. People do not have the money to spend on groceries because they are not working. Mines weekly announce they are closing, they are laying off personnel. If something is not done soon, there will be no more mining industry.
It is time that Canadians realized that something has to change and that message has to be relayed to the government. This bill, Bill C-20, which allows the government to withdraw all funding from just about all programs is not acceptable.
I hope that when we get to vote on clauses 8, 9 and 10 of this bill, we all rise and support these amendments put forward by my colleague from Essex-Windsor. It is clear to me that employers and employees cannot afford any more taxation of any kind if we are going to survive. If we are really sincere about creating jobs I think this government has to start spending some money in the right places.
There is no doubt in any Canadian's mind that we have to pay taxes in this country. We are willing to pay those taxes. How the money is spent is what we do not like. If the money is spent in the right place, we will not need subsidization. We will not need the government to bail us out all the time because we will have a system in which money will be regenerated and turned back into the organizations creating this money.
In conclusion, I hope that when we get to the amendments of clauses 8, 9 and 10 of Bill C-20, we all rise and support them.
