Mr. Speaker, this week marks the first annual white ribbon campaign. The campaign has been organized to help end violence against women and to heighten the awareness of men to this ever-growing problem.
Violence against women takes many forms, including physical and sexual assault, psychological and emotional abuse. It also threatens women of all ages, culture and backgrounds. When we look at the recent rash of violent acts committed by men against women it would seem that the word "civilized" is not part of our vocabulary.

December 2, 1991
Women are being gunned down, knifed, and beaten in record numbers but this is not a new phenomenon. It has been going on for quite some time.
I would encourage my male colleagues in this House, and all men across Canada for that matter, to take a leadership role in stopping this madness. It is up to us to give victims some hope. We must challenge conventional attitudes and behaviour. We must instil in our youth a new way of looking at humanity. We cannot stay silent any longer because, as with other atrocities, we become as guilty as the offender.
This week has been designated to raise awareness of the issue, but we cannot forget about the remaining 51 weeks in the year. I hope all men will wear a white ribbon to indicate their support for this cause. The country may not be covered with white snow, but we can cover it with white ribbons.

subtopic: ST. ANDREW'S CHURCH ON THE RED
ST. ANDREW'S CHURCH ON THE RED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to congratulate the efforts of the congregation of St. Andrew's Church on the Red.
The people of this church under the leadership of Father Stephen Sharman and with the help of the Government of Canada are about to begin the restoration of the oldest stone church in western Canada.
At a time when we are all concerned about where we are going, it is important to know where we have been. The efforts of the people of St. Andrew's on the Red will assure us of this very important part of our history.

Mr. Speaker, it has now been two years since the tragedy at the Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal. Since that time the war against women has continued. Men continue to abuse, neglect, harass, assault, and murder women. We as men must take on the work of educating ourselves in
order to understand sexism and speak out and challenge sexism in our daily lives.
We must work to pressure governments to increase funding for rape crisis centres, for shelters for battered women, and for comprehensive educational programs for men in positions of authority such as the judiciary, police departments and, indeed, in this House.
Men must take responsibility for the violence they have perpetrated in our homes and in our streets. This week is a time to commit ourselves to change, to speaking out, to helping out through donations and action. This week hundreds of men have worked to initiate the white ribbon campaign. Men across Canada are urged to hang a white ribbon from their house, their car, or at their work place, and to wear a white ribbon.
The white ribbon symbolizes a call for all men to lay down their arms in the war against our sisters. We must heed that call.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join my two hon. friends from across the way on the same topic.
I do not think any caring Canadian men can condone violence against women. What is difficult for many of us is to accept the premise that all men, including those who would never lift a finger against anyone, are partially responsible for this violence. This is the rationale behind the white ribbon campaign which runs from today until this Friday, the second anniversary of the tragic and troubling Montreal massacre.
I rise today as one man in Canadian society to say that I fully accept my responsibility to try and be a part of the solution to this problem. The best result of this campaign will be an increased awareness among all of us that sexism in any form, from jokes to harassment to violence itself, is unacceptable.
It is time that the least we can do is say that we are all very sorry.

Mr. Speaker, we in this House are very happy that the American hostage in Lebanon, Joseph Cicippio, has been released today. He was freed hours after Israel released 25 Arab prisoners.
There are only a few western hostages left in captivity and we have hopes that their ordeals will end in the coming weeks, if not days.
Besides the increasing good will developing in the Middle East, the key to their release has been constant pressure and relentless efforts by the international community.
Unfortunately, our joy is not complete. A Canadian woman, Mrs. Henriette Haddad, has been held hostage in Lebanon for more than six years. To this point, despite meetings with the family, the minister responsible for external affairs has refused to even put Mrs. Haddad's name on the list of hostages.
As the family told my colleague, the member for Winnipeg South Centre this week, the Canadian government does not even acknowledge that Mrs. Haddad is a hostage.
Our government has a duty to stand up for our citizens, as we have seen the American and other governments do over the hostage takings in Lebanon. We want Mrs. Haddad to be freed and we want the Canadian government to demand international pressure for her release as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the Ukrainian community of my riding welcomed the results of the independence referendum in their home country with great pride, joy and hope. This democratic exercise gave the Ukrainian people an opportunity to clearly express their sovereign will after 350 years of injustice and forced union.
Of course, President Gorbachev made threats. "Without Ukraine, there is no union, and without union, there will be neither social peace nor market economy and the country will sink into ethnic strife and anarchy", he said.
Instead, we see a new democratic country being bom, one that is open, tolerant toward its minorities and ready to associate on a normal basis of mutual interest rather than in a dominant/dominated relationship.
I hope that Ukrainian independence will be recognized immediately by Canada and all countries in the world.
I also wish to deplore our government's decision not to include the hon. member for Calgary Northeast, who is of Ukrainian origin, in the Canadian parliamentary delegation to supervise the referendum, even though he was officially invited and he is a knowledgeable observer of Ukraine's democratic evolution.

Mr. Speaker, another step toward Canada's green future was taken last Friday with the launching of the National Wildlife Strategy. The strategy, part of Canada's green plan, will protect wildlife diversity, conserve wildlife habitat and safeguard healthy ecosystems.
Efforts to recover populations of endangered species will be stepped up. Plans are in the works to identify habitat to protect national wildlife areas and migratory bird sanctuaries. Significant wetlands will be protected.
Research schedules on wildlife diseases, ecology and toxicology will be accelerated. The new National Wildlife Strategy goes hand in hand with new legislation before the House. The Wild Animal and Plant Protection Act is designed to protect wildlife, particularly endangered species from illegal trading and poaching. Several partnerships are emerging to save wildlife and wild places.
Governments, community groups and individuals are all working toward that common goal. The federal government is proud to be part of such a widespread commitment to wildlife.

December 2, 1991
I urge all members of the House and all Canadians to support these and other green plan projects contributing to a healthy environment.

Mr. Speaker, Goal 100 is a pilot project in employment partnership developed under the Industry Education Council in Hamilton. This project is geared to improving the success and cost effectiveness of employment related services for people with disabilities.
Small businesses under the leadership of Don Fell of Fell Fab Products in Hamilton have a remarkable commitment to this initiative. Twenty of these business champions aim to find 100 jobs for people with disabilities by the end of 1991.
The employment consortium evolved around this project is unique in Canada. Six sectors-employment, labour, service, consumer, education and resources-are identifying problems and opportunities, and co-ordinating existing federal, provincial and regional programs.
There are approximately 25,000 disabled job seekers in the Hamilton-Wentworth area. With the help of companies involved in Goal 100, many of these people will be able to leave the welfare ranks and join the employment ranks.
Congratulations to Hamilton business persons for their efforts in enabling disadvantaged individuals to become productive workers in today's and tomorrow's labour market.
Let them stand as examples to other employers-
The hon. member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, Premier Bourassa deplores the accusations of favouring Quebec that circulated last week in the Commons following the announcement of an industrial development agreement between Quebec and Ottawa. He says that such charges are completely unjustified. From this September to next June, $2.9 billion will be given in agricultural assistance for the grains sector, mainly to the western provinces.
Mr. Bourassa pointed out that this will bring the total for this kind of aid since 1985 to $20 billion. "No paltry sum", said he.
For several months, the Conservative members from Quebec together with the Minister of National Health and Welfare have shown the Cabinet that Quebec is entitled to its share for economic recovery in that province.
The statements made last week by NDP members, a Liberal member from Newfoundland and the Reform Party in Ottawa are a lot of nonsense.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, December 1, approximately 80 per cent of Ukrainians voted yes in a referendum which affirmed the Ukrainian Parliament's August 24 declaration of independence.
Over 6,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent who live in my constituency of Parkdale-High Park call on the Canadian government to recognize Ukrainian independence today, and to begin establishing full diplomatic relations.
Mr. Kravchuk, on his recent visit to Canada, assured us that nuclear weapons in Ukraine will remain under the control of a collective interdependent defence alliance until they are fully dismantled. He said that his independent Ukraine will guarantee equal rights to Russians, Jews and other minority groups.
I recommend that the government bring in a resolution to this Chamber today recognizing Ukraine as the world's newest independent nation, representing 52 million people and Europe's fourth largest geographical area

Mr. Speaker, there are many unsung heroes working diligently to promote the unity of Canada.
One of them is Jim Taylor of Toronto in his billboard campaign, now travelling through Atlantic Canada. He gained great support in my riding last Friday for his declaration: "My Canada includes Quebec".
December 2, 1991

Another is a group of singing and dancing students from Fredericton called "Characters Incorporated". Over the past several months, they have toured large parts of our country to inspire pride in Canada through their outstanding performances.
Along the way, they have collected an impressive tribute of signed commitments to Canada from many corner of the country. In due course, they will be presenting that tribute to Parliament through the Prime Minister.
These kinds of initiatives represent the power of public opinion. People do care about Canada, and purposes like these should be encouraged and supported at every stage in the constitutional cause. May every Canadian follow these examples.

Mr. Speaker, over the weekend, the people of Ukraine made a historic decision. My colleague, the member for Edmonton East, who was in Ukraine as part of a Canadian delegation to observe the elections, confirmed this morning that the people of Ukraine have overwhelmingly chosen to chart their own destiny.
This decision is being celebrated not only in Ukraine but also by hundreds of thousands of sons and daughters of Ukraine who live here in Canada.
I urge the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs to make sure Canada is among the first countries to give official recognition to this most recent addition to the world community of independent nations.
Now is the ideal time for the cultural and economic links between our nations to be strengthened. I can think of no better way to celebrate the 100 years of Ukrainian settlement in Canada than by reaffirming the historic links between our countries today.
Today is a pivotal day for the people of Ukraine. Let us make sure that Canada is there to assist them in the challenges ahead.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week on a tour of the Peace country, Preston Manning, leader of the Reform Party of Canada announced his party would abolish northern tax benefits.
For many years, many of his strongest supporters made themselves rich by taking the profits from our oil and gas fields home with them. Northern benefits have let the hard working people of the north keep just a few of those dollars at home.
I call on Preston Manning to stop listening to the guys with the bucks and help those without. The northern benefits puts money in the jeans of the men and women who toil in Canada's northern communities.
I will be contacting reeves, mayors, MLAs, MPs and other northern community leaders. Getting the northern tax benefit was only half the battle. Now the fight is to keep it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday, the Maurice Lamoureux egg candling centre of St. Isidore closed its doors, with the loss of 34 jobs in my riding. It is the second time in a month that St. Isidore de Prescott, with a population of 500, has been hit in that way. This shutdown is in addition to several others in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
I take the opportunity today to repeat the request I made many times in this House. Eastern Ontario needs a regional development program to fight chronic unemployment in our area. My constituents and I are still waiting. They are waiting for a favorable response from this government.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce details of the Canadian Lung Association's annual Christmas seal campaign.
The Lung Association, Canada's oldest national voluntary health organization, was formed in 1900. Although its early focus was with the prevention of tuberculosis, there are now other serious lung diseases that demand its attention. Deaths due to asthma have increased 163 per cent among people of the ages 15 to 34 since the early 1970s.
The Lung Association aims to improve these serious health conditions in Canada through research, education, patient services and the promotion of healthy living. The country-wide annual Christmas seal campaign represents the major financial support for the work of the association.
In London-Middlesex the Lung Association has helped 25,900 people: asthmatics, chronic lung disease, students smoking cessation program, a resource library, et cetera, with 180 volunteers. They would like to have more. Dedicated professionals such as Dr. Neville Lef-coe and others at Victoria Hospital are certainly working actively in this field.
The Lung Association of Canada has initiated the appreciation program for tobacco free pharmacies.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Leader of the Opposition made some statements about referendums. He suggested that a referendum be held on the same day that Quebec holds its referendum. He added that if English Canada said no in that referendum, the status quo would prevail. "We will have the Constitution that we have", he said.
A referendum is not a game. The Leader of the Opposition should stop annoying Quebecers unnecessarily. A referendum law is a way to break a deadlock, to use "in case". It is not to provoke Quebecers, much less to force them into something.
Furthermore, the Leader of the Opposition must understand one thing: You cannot hold a national referendum and if it fails pretend that nothing happened. There will be no third chance.

Mr. Speaker, on November 30, 1942, the residents of Winnipeg North Centre sent Stanley Knowles to the House of Commons. He is still here and he deserves our congratulations and our appreciation.
As a young person growing up on the outskirts of Winnipeg, I knew very little of party politics, but I heard many people talking about Stanley: Stanley for decent pensions; Stanley for working people; Stanley for poor women; Stanley for the unemployed, disposessed, the forgotten of our society. Stanley Knowles was a symbol then. He is an institution now. He represented and still represents a philosophy of service, of dedication and of sacrifice to others. Stanley Knowles was defeated just once, but even during that break he continued to work for the cause of social justice. Now, as he starts his 50th year in Ottawa, we, along with many other Canadians, express our best wishes to Stanley Knowles, a true person of the people.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister.
Today, the premiers of New Brunswick, Ontario and Manitoba, who represent all three national political parties in Canada, came together to urge the federal government to stop ignoring the economy and to convene an immediate First Ministers' Conference on the economy.
December 2, 1991

Will the Prime Minister immediately convene a First Ministers' Conference on the economy as requested by these three First Ministers.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance will be meeting with provincial finance ministers on December 12 and 13 for two days of intensive consultation precisely in regard to economic matters.
I have been holding bilateral meetings with first ministers, Premier Bourassa, Premier Rae. I will meet with Premier Romanow, Premier Harcourt, Premier Getty, and Premier Wells next week and will be making sure that during this cycle that we meet with all of the first ministers.
I will certainly be guided by their advice and be guided as well by the advice of the Minister of Finance after he meets with his provincial colleagues for two days of meetings and gives us a recommendation in regard to the usefulness and the effectiveness of such a meeting.
Therefore, I will be happy to report back to my hon. friend just as soon as these meetings are concluded. We will obviously do what is the best for Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Today, Mr. Speaker, 650,000 men and women must count on food banks for their daily bread. These people cannot wait any longer. Last week, the Prime Minister had a meeting with the premier of Ontario, and after that meeting, the premier of Ontario asked for a conference. Doesn't the Prime Minister think it would be time to show that he is very concerned that in a country like Canada, these people have to go to food banks? Is it not time to give them some hope and get all the Premiers together to find a way out of the recession?

Mr. Speaker, of course I want to give them hope, but not false hopes. Today interest rates in Canada are dropping. The inflation rate is going down. The IMF and the OECD have indicated that next year, Canada will rank first among all major industrialized countries in terms of economic growth. These are encouraging signs, despite
Oral Questions
our current problems. I would say that a lot depends on expenditure control and borrowing at the provincial level.
Even if we do have a meeting, I intend to examine very carefully, with the premiers and in public, the growth rate of their expenditures and loans and compare it with the federal government's record. I think you will see that the federal government has shown strong leadership in this area, and if we can persuade the provinces to follow our example, the economic recovery already under way will be stronger and more durable.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the problem we have had with this government is that for the past two years it has told us that it was to be a very short-term recession. Now we are in the second year, virtually a complete second year. Some 145,000 people had to go to food banks in Toronto alone last month and almost half of them were children.
When will this government stop fighting inflation and look at the other side of the coin. People in Canada need jobs in order to stop going to food banks. When will this government stop fighting inflation and concentrate on finding jobs for people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I remind the hon. Leader of the Opposition that 108,000 new jobs were created in the months of September and October. We have today the composite index from Statistics Canada which records the sixth consecutive increase in the outlook. That is a broad measurement of the economy. It takes into consideration some 10 different components, all the way from the stock market to furniture.
The other thing that should be noted is the fact that in the third quarter, while the growth was not as strong as we would have liked to have seen it, in the goods producing sector, there was a 5.2 per cent growth. I think that should be signs for encouragement, a 17.2 per cent increase in residential investment, the increase in jobs, the continuing reduction in interest rates, the continuing decline in inflation which will provide the lower income

Oral Questions
groups and the people on fixed incomes with that kind of security.
So it is not all gloom and doom. I think we are poised for a good rate of growth in 1992 as reflected by the projection of the IMF, the OECD, the Conference Board of Canada and others.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. October was yet another milestone for this government.

We now have a record number of bankruptcies and people who are obliged to use food banks. Among those who do, one out of five lost his or her job last year and has exhausted his or her unemployment insurance benefits.
Will the minister admit that his government's cuts in unemployment insurance have caused a transfer of this social burden to charitable organizations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously any bankruptcy is disturbing. We are, of course, concerned by the level of bankruptcies. The fact of the matter is with interest rates declining, the fact that it seems to have bottomed out, there are indications that we have seen the worst in terms of bankruptcies and we continue to look at some positive trends. The most positive trend is the continuing decline in interest rates.
I might say that this recession compared to 1981-82 in so far as bankruptcies makes this look very mild by comparison.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. When the Minister of Finance told the country to expect little improvement in the jobless rate for yet another year, thousands of Canadians were left to calculate how long they could hold out before declaring personal bankruptcy and join the crowd at their local food bank.
I ask the minister to announce that his government will no longer disown the unemployed and the poor and will now try to rescue the casualties of the Tory fiscal plague.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated, 108,000 new jobs were created during the months of September and October. It is expected that over 300,000 new jobs will be generated in 1992. The combination of that without the increase in the labour force, the expansion of the labour force, would result in a 2 per cent decline in the unemployment rate.
However, because of the large participation rate that the Canadian work force is involved in, it becomes a much more difficult challenge. I remind the hon. member that in terms of participation, Canada has the highest participation rate in the labour force of any country in the industrialized world and so our challenges are therefore greater.
I repeat, we must get the fundamentals right if we are going to have sustainable growth with price stability. That means long term growth and secure jobs for the future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Today Statistics Canada reports that in fact we do have a slowdown in the economy from last month. This simply confirms what millions of Canadians know, millions of Canadians for whom the recession is very far from over.
Often the finance minister has pointed to increases in corporate profits as an indication that the recession is over. I would ask the finance minister and the Prime Minister to look at the number of lay-offs this week alone, 139 jobs lost by Norsk Hydro; 2,000 lost jobs at IBM; 1,300 jobs at Town & Country Stores across the country; and CN bracing for more losses.
When will the Prime Minister begin to take into account the real victims of the recession, those who are without jobs and need to have some hope in the future, and put forth a plan to provide jobs for Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated, the only way to secure long-term growth, prosperity and permanent jobs is to get at the fundamentals, the fundamentals of bringing down interest rates, bringing down inflation. Consolidating and managing the fiscal challenge is really the only way that we can hope to ever achieve the kind of long term growth and stability that the hon. member refers to.

I remind her that this government has helped in creating a climate that generated 1.6 million new jobs, the highest record of job creation of any country in the industrialized world. We have gone through a period of adjustment and retrenchment; we are going through that. As a matter of fact the Governor of the Bank of Canada today indicated in his speech the main point, and I quote: "What I wish to convey from this monetary policy perspective is that Canada is now much better placed to enjoy good economic"-
The hon. member for Yukon. [Translation]

I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker.
When this government is optimistic, it predicts that one Canadian out of ten will be unemployed next year. The government has no economic recovery plan for the
1.5	million Canadians who are unemployed and the 2 million who are on welfare. An economic policy that ensures that the banks make billions of dollars of profits while children go hungry is a policy that does not work.
I would like to ask the minister when this government will help the real victims of the recession, the unemployed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party can help in this area as well. If we look at the September growth figures there was a decline of .1 per cent. I think everyone shares the view that if it had not been for the disruptive strikes that occurred we probably would have had positive growth in September.
The former premier of British Columbia should know that because of the strikes we lost a lot of grain deliveries. That certainly affected our export position and that affected our merchandise trade balance.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance will not convince one Canadian that the poor management of this government is any excuse. Employee relations by this government are so bad that it was not even able to deal with its own employees. I want to say that is not the cause of the recession. The cause of
Oral Questions
the recession is government's policies. I want to say to the Minister of Finance that a recovery which does not put people back to work is not a recovery.
The Minister of Finance told us last week that in his budget consultations he was hearing that he was on the right track. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance to whom was he speaking? Was he just speaking to the bankers who made all those profits? How about speaking to those three million people who are out of work and on social assistance and asking for answers from that group of people? Has he spoken to them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be happy to answer that question.
I have heard it from anti-poverty groups, from the Paraplegic Association and from NAC, the National Action Committee. I have heard it from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I have heard it from the retailers. I have heard it from the farmers. I have heard it literally from a cross-section.
What are you doing about it?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: What are we doing about it? The fact of the matter is that everyone knows we have a fiscal deficit problem we inherited from the previous administration that must be dealt with.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister.
We are pleased to recognize that the Prime Minister took the step this morning of recognizing the independence of Ukraine.
Hear, hear.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister some questions to clarify the statement released by his office which says: "Canada will only open negotiations and will have to satisfy itself with respect to Ukraine's stated intentions on ensuring that nuclear weapons will remain under secure control that there will be compliance with existing arms control agreements" and so forth.

Oral Questions
It is our understanding that those assurances have already been given by the President of Ukraine, Mr. Kravchuk, in a letter to the Prime Minister this week. I want to ask the Prime Minister: What further conditions, what further assurances is the Prime Minister requiring before full embassy status is given to Kiev and the full diplomatic power of immigration and other negotiations are transferred to that post in Kiev?
Could the Prime Minister indicate what more it is that Canada is now looking for under these negotiations?

Mr. Speaker, when we saw the results of the vote in Ukraine, the government decided to recognize Ukraine as an independent state. That we have done and we have announced.
It is not unusual, pursuant to such a decision, for a country to open negotiations with regard to the establishment of diplomatic relations. In this case which is quite unusual Canada will wish to be satisfied with respect, for example, to the question of nuclear weapons that will remain under secure control until they are disposed of.
Overnight a country has become a nuclear power with nuclear weapons on its territory. Obviously, in the interests of effective bilateral relationships and in the interests of security, we are going to want to assure ourselves of the security of those weapons. We want them destroyed and/or removed and placed under secure control. This is an entirely normal process which we are informed the leadership of the Ukraine welcomes.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. I think it still begs the question as to whether this is an unqualified or qualified recognition. We would like to know what further assurances in addition to Mr. Kravchuk's letter the Prime Minister is looking for.
Furthermore, I think we all recognize that a newly independent country needs more than just recognition. It needs assistance for its economic security. It needs assurances on its own security, and particularly in the case of Ukraine this question of dismantling its nuclear weapons is very crucial.
We should all take account of the UN report released this morning saying that there could be major unrest in eastern Europe if there is not another Marshall Plan.
In addition to these negotiations about nuclear weapons, is Canada prepared to offer to Ukraine substantial new economic assistance and in particular respond to the request we made this morning that Canada help in the conversion of its nuclear warheads to peaceful purposes?

We do
not want the nuclear warheads converted. We want them done away with. That is what we want.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend asks two questions. On the first one the answer is contained in the first line of the statement: "Prime Minister Brian Mulroney today announced that Canada had decided to recognize Ukraine as an independent state". The recognition issue is resolved.
With regard to the second question raised in regard to future economic assistance and so on, in my meetings with President Kravchuk prior to to the election when he visited with me in Ottawa, I conveyed to him the view that after the election, and assuming certain results if that were the case, we would be dispatching senior public officials of the Government of Canada to meet with the officials of the newly elected government to deal precisely with the questions raised by my hon. friend.
The last line of the release deals precisely with that: "The Prime Minister confirmed that senior officials will be going to Kiev in the coming days to convey Canada's position and to begin the process of negotiations", which takes in as well the matters raise by my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Eighteen months ago, the government promised to do environmental assessments of all its policies. The green plan reinforced this promise.

So far, however, no comprehensive environmental assessment has been made of policies at the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The minister simply refuses to co-operate. Why?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister of energy is not in a position where he does not co-operate. He is co-operating.
On any issue that comes before cabinet through the regular documentation we have to satisfy and I as minister of energy I have to satisfy the environmental conditions. That is a condition of cabinet decision making. I am doing it.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
Energy policy is a critical indicator of a government's commitment to sustainable development. The minister's refusal, his cabinet's refusal to allow an environmental assessment of the government's energy policy, demonstrates not only a lack of concern for the environment but is poor economic policy as well.
The question is very clear. When will the government produce the environmental evaluation of his department's energy choices, an evaluation that was promised clearly and unequivocally 18 months ago?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if there is any change in the policy position and if cabinet makes that decision, part of that decision-making process will be the environmental considerations. As we have said before that remains and no change has taken place.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance and Deputy Prime Minister.
Most Canadians readily understand the need to compensate some individuals for the risks they take in providing information on drug smuggling, murder or
Oral Questions
conspiracy to the RCMP or the Security Intelligence Service. What is less clear is why Fisheries and Oceans, Environment Canada, and Revenue Canada are developing paid confidential informant programs.
My question for the Minister of Finance is: Would he explain why there are departments that are allowed to operate such programs without placing the costs in the estimates before Parliament, something the Minister of Finance is directly responsible for?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister of fisheries I can tell the House that I will be pleased to take my hon. friend's representations into account and report back to him as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance. The minister of fisheries is here, so the Solicitor General's response was not all that helpful.
Oh, oh.
Maybe we are going to have to start over. The hon. member for Skeena.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. The minister of fisheries has obviously had a very close shave.
My supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance, because this is an important auditing function that he handles. There are now at least five ministries on that side of the House involved in informant programs.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance whether or not he would agree that rather than operating the bounty hunter programs which are now being operated by Fisheries, Revenue, and soon by Environment Canada, with secret bank accounts and secret telephone numbers, does he not think it would be better to set up some hot-lines where Canadians can advise the departments of illegal activities that they are aware of?
Will the minister assure this House that by the end of today he will table all the budgets of all the ministries on that side of the House that have informant programs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member referred to the Main Estimates maybe I can be of some assistance.

Oral Questions
I would like to tell him that the payments that are made to individuals under the enforcement programs of various departments are considered to be operating expenses.
There is no separate line item in the estimates for that particular purpose, but the amounts are available as the hon. member knows very well because he was provided with the answers when he asked the question.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
As we prepare to mark the second anniversary of the tragedy at Ecole Polytechnique, the incidence of violence against women on Canadian campuses is on the increase. In particular the statistics on date rape are very frightening.
Will the Prime Minister convene a meeting of university presidents nation-wide to develop with them a concrete plan including education and enforcement policies to stop violence against women on Canadian campuses?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry but the Minister responsible for the Status of Women is away on government business today. I will certainly bring the matter to her attention on her return.
One knows and understands how hard she has worked to make all of us much more aware of the very debilitating effect of violence and harassment of women and how much we have to do.
In this particular week, as we come up to the commemoration of the second anniversary of the event, all of us will be thinking of the young women whose lives were snuffed out before their future even unfolded.
I am sure the minister responsible will be addressing herself to this subject on her return to the House.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his answer, but I posed my question then and I pose it again to the Prime Minister of Canada with this supplementary.

Is the Prime Minister prepared to promise financial support for Canadian universities so that they can develop policies to fight date rape?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member for Halifax must know that recently in Edmonton, I announced the funding of three university chairs to research violence against women. I do not think she meant what she said; I think that she is talking about co-operation between training centres, particularly at the university level. This was extremely well received by women's groups when I made the announcement in Edmonton because I think that it is a policy that will help determine-and I agree fully with the hon. member-exactly what must be done in Canadian society to find ways to fight violence against women. The same goes for all forms of violence against women and children; we have policies involving hundreds of millions of dollars as an expression of our commitment.
Again, I repeat that we have made commitments to women's groups. I personally announced the funding next year of three university chairs for violence against women. I think that shows the government's intention to do something in that area.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Last night and tonight millions of Canadians are viewing an electrifying television documentary on the brutal slaying of Manitoba native Helen Betty Osborne.
Her death became the focus of the aboriginal justice inquiry of Manitoba which released its report last summer. This report made several recommendations for the federal government.
Why is the government delaying its response and ignoring the many ways through many departments that it can make justice a reality for Canada's aboriginal community?

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is quite aware of the report to which my hon. friend refers.
In fact I met as well with the minister of justice of Manitoba to discuss the federal report. At the present time the recommendations in the report are being studied by the RCMP. I can assure my hon. friend that this is not a matter where we are delaying in any way.
We want to provide a thoughtful and thorough response to this very important inquiry.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister, the Solicitor General.
It is hard to believe that after three months and 150 recommendations on one of the most serious criminal issues and one of the most serious social issues in this country the minister cannot find one recommendation to start with.
When will this government begin to deal with these very serious problems?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the various efforts by the government to deal with this very serious problem have been alluded to today in previous answers.
I can assure my friend that the 150 recommendations are to be taken seriously. We are not in a mood to delay on this important issue. They are being taken seriously. The government will provide a response when the matter is brought forward.
We can only respond to the recommendations that are ours. It is a report made in the purview of the minister of justice of the province of Manitoba. Naturally we want to take instruction from that report and react to as many recommendations as we can.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the minister of health.
The federal government's response on Thursday to the recommendations of the report of the standing committee on health has been disappointing, particularly at a time when Canadians are looking for strong reasons to remain as part of a federal Canada.
Could the minister tell the House why his government supports the recommendations of the Liberal and Conservative committee members for the wholesale renegotiation of medicare at a time when Canadians are saying very clearly that they want national medicare with national standards and they do not want Bill C-20 and the continued federal cutbacks to financing of medicare?
Order, order.
I listened to the whole question because I did not want to intervene too quickly, but I think that question goes right into the workings of the committee and I think it is out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs.
Back since September in my community we have had a group of volunteers, 20-odd people who have been meeting, discussing and holding public forums on constitutional proposals.
In the last while the work plan of the joint House and Senate parliamentary committee has changed and there has been a creation of constitutional conferences.
I am wondering if the minister could tell the House the status of these constitutional conferences and what reflection it will have on the small community based committees.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to indicate today that there will be five constitutional conferences on consecutive weekends in cities across Canada starting on January 17 in Halifax, sponsored by a number of independent institutes in the country: the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, the Canada West Foundation, the C. D. Howe Institute, the Institute for Research into Public Policy and the Niagara Institute.
Those conferences will call together experts plus, through a process worked out with the institutes, an effective representation of the general public. That will allow us to continue the process of building consensus on improvements for the proposals brought forward and tabled by the Prime Minister in September.

December 2, 1991
Oral Questions
The fifth conference will be a concluding conference organized jointly by the Government of Canada and the five sponsoring institutes.
There had been talk, as the House will know, about a conference on aboriginal matters. I have had meetings with leaders of the four national aboriginal organizations. At the moment it is not their preference to proceed with a discussion on aboriginal issues, although that question is being discussed.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The California Public Utilities Commission recently announced a decision which has the effect of abrogating long-term private contracts between Canadian natural gas producers on one hand and California consumers on the other. This would be very serious for our natural gas industry.
When will this minister respond to the strong and frequent representations from Alberta P.C. members of this House and take action to defend the interests of Canadian natural gas producers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for his question.
This is a very serious issue. I would hope that all members of the House would join with the government in the actions that we plan to unveil tomorrow in Calgary. It is an issue that relates to the sanctity of contracts.
Natural gas has been provided to the California market. Since 1961 various administrations in this place have supported that type of export.
Tomorrow we will be joined by the province of Alberta, by the industry, and I hope by members on both sides of this House so that the sanctity of contracts remains and that the actions we propose tomorrow will be endorsed by this House.

Mr. Speaker, in the House last week the parliamentary secretary to the minister of fisheries stated that his minister was aware of what the fishermen and plant workers were saying regarding the inadequacy of the Atlantic Fisheries Catch Failure Program in which people who have been involved in the fisheries all their lives have not been able to qualify, or if they qualify there is no funding for the program.
If the minister is aware of this, I would like to ask him what he is going to do about it and when.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my information that everyone in the areas affected who has a relationship to the fishery in accordance with the rules that were laid down is being looked after in this program. If there are any who have been missed, they can be included once they provide the information that shows they have a reasonable attachment to the fishery.
There is no problem with respect to money. The difficulty is that there are a fairly sizeable number of people without any reasonable attachment to the fishery who also have not qualified for unemployment insurance or who in the next month or two are coming off the unemployment insurance program and will then be looking for assistance. That is where the difficulty comes from.
Those with a reasonable attachment to the fishery, I believe have been looked after.

Mr. Speaker, last week at the same time in response to a question the Prime Minister said that the $39 million, he claimed, provided for Newfoundland was not enough. In fact the $39 million was for three provinces. So Newfoundland and Labrador got considerably less than that.
Anyway the Prime Minister said: "That is not enough for Newfoundlanders". The Prime Minister knows that there are some inadequacies in the program and the minister knows there are some inadequacies in the program despite what he just said.
December 2, 1991

Could I call on the Prime Minister to order his minister of fisheries to come to the aid of Newfoundland plant workers and fishermen who need more money, to provide programs for them that they badly need and rightly deserve?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in connection with this program, this program has provided funds to assist fishermen affected by catch failure wherever they were in Atlantic Canada, including Nova Scotia. The lion's share, if we might call it that, of the assistance has gone to Newfoundland and Labrador because this was the main area of catch failure.
For example, in connection with funding provided for
14.000	additional tonnes of herring to be purchased to give more work to fishermen and fish plant workers,
10.000	tonnes of that was allocated to Newfoundland and
4.000	to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. We are trying to be as fair as we can be.
The Prime Minister of course is heavily in favour of assistance to anyone living anywhere in Canada where there is a demonstrated need, as the actions of the government have shown.

[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Inuktitut]

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister. For 50 years the Lubicon Lake Indian band has been trying to settle its land claims. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has said he is committed to resolving this claim.
Why then have there been no negotiations with the Lubicon Cree since 1989, and can the Prime Minister explain why the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development created and funded last year a new band in the area claimed by the Lubicon band?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's ongoing concern on this particular issue, just as the Minister of
Oral Questions
Indian Affairs and Northern Development also has a concern.
We have been working with the bands to try to reach an agreement on this.
Baloney.
We are ready to sit down with them when they are ready to come back to the table and we will follow up on this.
I wonder if the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast would apologize to the hon. minister for shouting out comments in the middle of her answer.
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the minister, but I do not think her answer was very candid.
I do not think that that is any apology at all. This is the very thing where we are getting into difficulty. I have asked the hon. member to withdraw unequivocally.
I am not going to go beyond that. I have apologized.
Would the hon. member rise to his feet and let me know what he is saying? I cannot hear him otherwise.
Mr. Speaker, I am familiar with the Lubicon file too and I think that the question was fair. I do not think the answer was a fair response.
I think the hon. member's intervention is completely improper.
I agree it was a bit strong.
I would ask the hon. member to make it quite clear, at least to the Chair, that the intervention was improper and that it is withdrawn.

Oh, oh.

An order to create another new band, the Loon Lake band in the northern part of the land claimed by the Lubicon band, is apparently in the office of the Minister

Point of Order
of Indian Affairs and Northern Development awaiting his signature.
In order to demonstrate this government's commitment to a fair settlement with the Lubicon band, will the Prime Minister today order the minister not to sign this order and to resume negotiations with the Lubicon people immediately?
Mr. Speaker, I rise again, I hope uninterrupted this time, to say that this government-
Oh, oh.
The Chair has intervened. I would ask the hon. minister to put as clear an answer as is possible without getting into undue argument.

As I mentioned earlier, I know the member's very true concern about the particular issue. I will take his last question back to the minister of Indian affairs if he returns tomorrow and discuss it with him.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare and concerns funding for the national AIDS strategy. As the minister knows we have been celebrating World AIDS Day and attempting to deal with this issue in a more constructive way.
The minister will know of the excellent work of AIDS support groups across Canada and will know that funding for these groups under ACAP was cut from was cut from $7 million to $6.4 million for 1991.
I wonder if the minister can confirm today that this $600,000 will be reinstated forthwith so that these AIDS support groups can continue with their critically important work.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the views of the member about the World AIDS Day yesterday. I believe that all Canadians have to be concerned about this terrible disease.
Concerning ACAP, I said to the committee when I appeared on October 30 that I was looking at the possibility of reallocating money already devoted to that file and that if there was a possibility of doing that for
19911 would, for this year. However, I can confirm that for 1992-1993 the budget will be $7 million.

Mr. Speaker, also as the minister knows, across Canada there are considerable inconsistencies in the treatment of AIDS and its availability and the cost of prescription drugs.
I wonder if the minister can indicate what steps he is taking to eliminate these inconsistencies so that those persons living with AIDS in Canada can receive the same accessibility to medical treatment no matter where they live.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are trying to work with the provinces on that kind of file. The member knows very well that prescription drugs are determined by the provinces. They make those decisions.
The health care system is made in a way that we can provide as much as we can. As I was told in Europe recently, we have the best health care system in the world. For that reason we are trying to provide the same service all across the country, but of course there are problems in the kind of treatment and the kind of prescription drugs. For example, the problem is not the same in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal as it is in any other province. That is why once again we are working with the provinces.
I believe the question is well put. It should be dealt with in that way by those provinces.

Mr. Speaker, continued bloodshed in Croatia is unacceptable to my constituents and my question regarding this is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Could she please tell this House the status of efforts to put a UN peacekeeping force into Yugoslavia to control the Serbian army, and will Canada commit troops to help protect Croatia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has been in the forefront of this issue from the beginning, particularly in urging the Security Council and the United Nations to become engaged in stopping the violence.
December 2, 1991

We will indeed put peacekeeping troops into the area. Mr. Vance, representing the Secretary-General, is in Belgrade now and his assistant is in Zagreb. We are in constant touch with the United Nations and with Mr. Vance. I spoke to him just before he left and told him at that point that Canada would be part of a peacekeeping effort, as the Prime Minister had said publicly and as we had urged the Security Council to take on. There will have to be another resolution at the Security Council I understand when Mr. Vance returns. We are in touch with our people at the UN as well as through our posts in all the Security Council countries to urge them to establish this so that we can get started.

The member was asking a question about the government's response to a committee report tabled in this House. This report therefore is no longer the property of the committee but is something of which the House has been seized. December 2, 1991

Mr. Speaker,
I am pleased to table a petition from residents of my riding and other areas of metropolitan Toronto urging the minister of immigration to issue minister's permits for spouses and dependent children of persons who have been determined to be convention refugees and allow these families to be reunited in Canada for inland processing.
If this were done, we would limit tragic situations such as the four Gunajothy children between the ages of 5 and 12 who have been waiting for three years in a hotel room in Colombo in terror, without a permanent care giver, while their parents achieved refugee status and were landed last June.
It is six months now that they have been sponsored and they have not even received medical instructions. These children will be Canadian citizens and they will remember their years of fear, loneliness and waiting.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-20, an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament on February 26, 1991, be read the third time and passed.
December 2, 1991

Government Orders
He said: I rise today to speak on third reading of Bill C-20. As everyone knows, this bill implements the measures announced in the February 1991 budget by the then minister of finance.
Bill C-20 implements several spending restraint and deficit control measures. It affects the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangement Act, the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act and the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Before I discuss the details of the bill let me, at the outset thank all those who participated on the committee for their work, their suggestions and their useful comments.
I listened this morning very carefully to the comments of my colleagues from both opposition parties. The legislation should be understood in the broad context of the government's over-all economic agenda. Measures proposed in the February budget set out in the plan for economic recovery are essential to restore strong, continuing growth that leads to the renewed prosperity that Canadians want.
The key to recovery is lower interest rates. It requires reduction in expectations and in inflation. Part of this comes from putting government finances firmly on course to a balanced budget and by restraining the operations of government. The budget plans for economic recovery support these goals through further tough discipline and government spending, deficit reduction and control of the government's operating costs.
The Minister of Finance today in Question Period mentioned that he is in the process of having pre-budget consultations with the broadest cross section of people in our country from all walks of life. I shared those pre-budget consultations with him last week in Toronto and they were represented by many groups.
All of those groups are experiencing in most instances financial problems at this period of time as they come through a recession. They sent one message loud and clear from those consultations and that was to stick to what we are doing, we are on the right track and we will be proven right. Interest rates are coming down and inflation is down at an annualized rate now that is beyond the goals that were set by the Government of Canada.
They said that we are on the right track. For heaven's sake do not backtrack. That came loud and clear. There were other suggestions from many of the groups which made representations on how we can improve the situation economically. There were suggestions for the upcoming 1992 spring budget, but generally that was the theme that came through loud and clear.
This bill talks to those policies we are implementing to ensure that we stay on the right track and to ensure that the young people coming behind us are not going to be paying all our bills. We will start making a dent in that huge debt that has been built up over a number years.
The measures before us today have important implications for federal-provincial fiscal arrangements and in particular the major transfers to two provinces.
I listened today to some figures that were thrown out by the opposition parties. I am not sure where they got the figures or what inflation rate they were basing then-figures on. We heard a wide range of figures thrown around today all of which are hypothetical and all of which are added or subtracted. They are primarily added or embellished on by the opposition. We are not sure where the accuracy of them can be found.
Today the federal government provides about $37 billion in financial support to provincial governments. There are three major transfer programs. The Established Programs Financing or EPF, equalization and the Canada Assistance Plan referred to as CAP. They account for over 90 per cent of all federal transfers to provinces or more than $34 billion for 1991-92.
That is a lot of money. That is about 20 or 25 per cent of the program spending that goes to the provinces. Bill C-20 which we are debating in third reading helps to bring the growth of federal-provincial transfers into line. I emphasize that it is the growth, not reductions, of these transfers that is being brought into line with the current fiscal realities by introducing limits to the growth of payments under the EPF. I think it is very important to understand that they continue to grow, maybe not at the rate the New Democratic Party or the Liberal Party or even the Conservative Party would like to see. It is especially not at the rate the provinces would like to see but within the fiscal realities that we are dealing with we believe they are realistic.

Government Orders
It is important to note that the government has not touched equalization. Transfers under this program to the less wealthy provinces have been exempted from the budget expenditure controls. Even with the measures proposed in the budget, growth in federal transfers is expected to run at 3.7 per cent annually between 1991-92 and 1995-96. That will be more than the rate of inflation during that period of time if our goals are reached and we believe they will be reached. This is in contrast to three per cent for all federal programs over the same period.
Bill C-20 brings the growth of federal-provincial transfers into line with these current fiscal realities which are much different than they were in the 1960s and the 1970s when our major transfer programs took their present form. Times change. The economy changes and situations change. The federal government has already announced and has started consultations with the provinces and Canadians generally on the reform of the major transfer system. The provinces have requested this. They want to assure funding as well. They are concerned about the system and we want to take a major look at that system. It has been guided by the principles that the new transfer system must be affordable.
It must protect provinces with lesser financial means. It must maintain the vital national public services expected by Canadians while providing accountability to the public.
The fearmongering that has been going on this morning by the New Democratic Party I think is totally unfair and unfounded. There has been screaming and moaning and groaning about our medicare system and how those nasty Tories want to do away with it. What utter nonsense. What poppycock. What socialist baloney. That is absolute nonsense. We have as much concern about the medicare system as anyone does.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: We want to bring it into the 21st century.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
That is exactly what we want to do. We want to assure that services are provided and that they are affordable. That is what it is all about.
For the New Democratic Party to say that this government is not concerned about medicare is totally false. It is absolutely totally false.

They were standing up not too long ago blaming the provinces for not spending the money on medicare that they get from the federal government.
That says to me that the federal government is giving the money and the provinces are not spending it on medicare. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot say that we are destroying the medicare system when the provinces are not spending the money they get for medicare on medicare. You cannot have it both ways over there. You just cannot do it. I will not buy the nonsense which is handed out to the Canadian public because it is just not true and the hon. member knows it.
